Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install · [LLM] Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the 5 SHA256 hashes associated with the Miasma/Hades June 2026 campaign are observed as either an executed binary or a file written to disk on an enrolled host. Catches the worm landing or running irrespective of the delivery vector (npm install, IDE folder open, PyPI import). Rationale: Uses the 5 SHA256 IOCs pre-extracted from the StepSecurity advisory. Cross-checked against Semgrep's Miasma v2 writeup and StepSecurity's Hades campaign writeup which confirm the same hash family. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating IOC in a sandbox VM enrolled to production tenant
  • Defender threat-intel sample auto-downloaded to MpCmdRun quarantine folder
  • Forensic analyst copying the sample to a triage share for review
  • SOAR enrichment pipeline storing the binary in an evidence bucket synced back to disk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\" and FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\evidence\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the host's last 24h DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents and confirm whether the hash was executed (process row) or only landed (file row). Identify the parent (npm.exe, node-gyp, python.exe) and the originating package/folder path. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device in Defender (Isolate Device), force-rotate any npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure tokens that lived on that host or in any repo the developer recently opened — assume tokens were exfiltrated. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on AccountUpn across all hosts for the same hash, then hunt UC2/UC3 (Phantom Gyp + Hades Bun) against the same user/devices to map full scope; review GitHub for any new workflow files or attacker-controlled repos.

Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' technique: a ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped into a package directory under node_modules that triggers code execution at the native build step of npm install, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script monitoring. Filters to package-manager parent processes so legitimate library development is not flagged. Rationale: Article explicitly names the 157-byte binding.gyp as the Phantom Gyp payload dropped during npm install. Size filter (50-500 bytes) plus the node_modules path plus the npm/yarn/pnpm parent are all article-derived; legitimate binding.gyp files in published packages are typically much larger and produced by the package author rather than dropped by tar extraction during install. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer authoring a genuinely tiny binding.gyp stub for a local native addon being tested under node_modules
  • tar.exe extracting a benign package whose author shipped a minimal binding.gyp (e.g. config-only)
  • pnpm content-addressable store unpacking many legitimate binding.gyp files during fresh install
  • Forensic analyst copying a malicious binding.gyp sample to a node_modules path for sandbox testing
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\node_modules\.pnpm\@types\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm publish" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp configure"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: open the file, read its content (it will be small JS/Python embedded inside the gyp action block), and identify the package directory it landed in. Capture the package name + version from the adjacent package.json. Step 2 — Contain: kill any running node-gyp / npm install on the host, isolate the device in EDR, and force-revoke the developer's NPM_TOKEN, GitHub PAT, AWS/Azure/GCP creds, and any tokens visible in process memory of the npm invocation. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the package name across the org to identify other developers who installed the same version; trigger UC1 hash search and UC6 Bun-exfil search; query npm registry for all versions of that package published in the last 7 days.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades on-import payload: python interpreter spawns Bun runtime download AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades PyPI execution chain: an obfuscated hook in a package's __init__.py runs at import time and fetches the standalone Bun JavaScript runtime (v1.3.13/1.3.14) from GitHub releases or bun.sh, then executes the _index.js payload. Pivot is python.exe as parent of curl/wget/bun or python making outbound HTTP to Bun distribution endpoints. Rationale: Article names the Bun runtime download as the Hades execution mechanism triggered from __init__.py; corroborating writeups (Orca, SocRadar, Rescana) pin the Bun versions to 1.3.13/1.3.14 and the dropper payload filename as _index.js. python -> bun.exe is highly unusual outside this campaign because python developers virtually never bootstrap a Bun runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://orca.security/resources/blog/hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack-poisons-19-python-packages-with-bun-based-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1105 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer experimentally calling out to Bun from a Python script (rare but possible for cross-runtime tooling)
  • Internal data-pipeline using a Python wrapper around a Bun script
  • Anaconda/conda-forge recipe builder fetching Bun as a build dependency
  • Sandbox/dynamic analysis tooling intentionally executing a Hades sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "conda-build" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Anaconda\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enumerate the python process's recent stdin/CWD and resolve which PyPI package was imported. Pull the package's __init__.py, decode the obfuscated one-liner, and confirm Bun download URL. Capture Bun binary SHA256 and the _index.js payload. Step 2 — Contain: isolate device in Defender, kill the bun.exe process tree, force-rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes tokens for the affected user; revoke any SSH keys present in ~/.ssh. Pull the package version from PyPI; report to PyPI security if not already taken down. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the resolved Bun download IP/URL across all hosts (DeviceNetworkEvents); search for the _index.js payload hash; check for follow-on GitHub repo creations by the user (worm C2 channel).
let HadesPkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools"]);
// Stage A: python parent spawns bun / fetcher referencing Bun distribution
let StageA = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
  | where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","node.exe")
  | where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux","bun-v1.3.13","bun-v1.3.14","_index.js");
// Stage B: python directly egressing to Bun distribution endpoints
let StageB = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("bun.sh","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, FileName="(network)", ProcessCommandLine="";
StageA
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl="", RemoteIP=""
| union StageB
| order by Timestamp desc
let StageA = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python(3|w)?\.exe$" or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\py\.exe$"
  | where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(bun|curl|wget|powershell|pwsh|node)\.exe$"
  | where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\bun\.exe$"
      or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux","bun-v1.3.13","bun-v1.3.14","_index.js")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Source="Process";
let StageB = ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where SrcUsername != "" and Url has_any ("bun.sh","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux")
  | join kind=inner (ImProcessCreate | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python(3|w)?\.exe$" | project DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ProcTime=TimeGenerated, ActingProcessCommandLine) on DvcHostname
  | where TimeGenerated between (ProcTime - 5m .. ProcTime + 5m)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName="python.exe", ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName="(network)", TargetProcessCommandLine=Url, Source="Network";
StageA | union StageB | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI Worm - Python Spawns Bun Runtime Downloader
id: 9e2f7b1c-4d6a-4f8b-b0c5-7e3d9f1a2b33
status: experimental
description: Detects python interpreter spawning a child process that downloads or invokes the Bun runtime, matching the Hades PyPI campaign's on-import payload (StepSecurity, June 2026).

Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the broader Miasma/Hades tactic of seeding editor and AI-assistant config files into a project so they execute when a developer opens the folder or starts a session. Detects writes of .vscode/tasks.json (runOn:folderOpen), .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, or .github/setup.js when the writer is git/npm/pip/tar (not the IDE itself) — meaning the file is arriving via a clone or install, not authored locally. Rationale: The article's Table 1 enumerates exactly these 7 file paths and their auto-execute triggers. Pivoting on package-manager/git as the writer eliminates the common FP of a developer manually authoring these files in the IDE — when git clone or npm install drops them, the file came from the published package itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/miasma-mini-shai-hulud-ai-agent-supply-chain-2026/ • https://complexdiscovery.com/when-the-worm-targets-the-assistant-miasma-turns-ai-coding-agents-into-the-trigger/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running git clone on a legitimate repo whose maintainer ships a .vscode/tasks.json for local dev tooling
  • npm install of a package that legitimately includes a .vscode/extensions.json or task config
  • pip install of an internal dev tooling package that ships .vscode files (rare but possible)
  • yarn workspace bootstrap that copies tasks.json from a template directory
  • CI agent fetching repo with .github/setup.js used for environment setup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "git clone https://github.com/<your-org>/" or FolderPath has @"\internal-template-repo\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the dropped file. For tasks.json, look for runOn:folderOpen + node/bun/curl/python invocation. For setup.mjs/setup.mdc/setup.js, examine the JS for obfuscated payloads or fetches to non-corp domains. Identify the originating package (look at adjacent package.json / requirements.txt / git remote origin). Step 2 — Contain: warn the developer NOT to open the folder in VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini; quarantine the file; if already opened, isolate the device, kill any spawned child processes, force-rotate the developer's tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source package name across the org; run UC1 hashes, UC3 (Bun runtime), UC6 (Bun outbound) on the same host; check git log on the repo for who/when added the file.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, @"\", FileName)
| where FullPath has_any (@"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.vscode\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
// Drop writes by the legitimate IDE — those are user authoring; keep writes by package managers / git / extractors
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git clone","git pull","git checkout","npm install","npm i ","pip install","yarn add","pnpm install")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FullPath, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.vscode\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(git|npm|node|pip|python(3)?|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|curl|wget|bun)\.exe$"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git clone","git pull","git checkout","npm install","pip install","yarn add","pnpm install")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script AIExploitation High
Detects the moment of execution for the editor/AI-tool auto-execute trigger — Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini parent-process spawning node/bun/python/powershell/cmd with a command line referencing tasks.json, setup.mjs, setup.mdc, .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, or .github/setup.js. This catches the worm running even if the dropping vector (UC4) was missed. Rationale: Article's Table 1 explicitly maps each file to its auto-execute trigger (runOn:folderOpen for tasks.json, SessionStart for .claude/setup.mjs, Custom rules load for .cursor/rules/setup.mdc). When the editor itself is the parent of an interpreter that loads one of these paths, the trigger has actually fired — much higher signal than just the file existing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/miasma-mini-shai-hulud-ai-agent-supply-chain-2026/
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's own .vscode/tasks.json running a legitimate build task on folder open
  • Claude Code SessionStart hook running an internal corp-approved setup.mjs
  • Cursor rules file loading a benign internal lint script
  • VS Code Remote SSH bootstrap spawning node for the remote server
  • Anaconda Python environment activation triggered by VS Code Python extension
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has @"\internal-corp-tooling\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--corp-trusted-folder")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: open the referenced setup script (setup.mjs/setup.mdc/tasks.json) and check for obfuscation, outbound fetches, or Bun runtime invocation. Identify the git remote of the project folder. Step 2 — Contain: kill the child process tree, close the IDE, isolate the device. Force-rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault tokens for the developer. Step 3 — Hunt: search across the fleet for the same project path / git remote being opened by other developers. Pivot on UC6 (Bun outbound) to find post-execution exfil. Add the dropped file's SHA256 to the IOC list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","devenv.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","devenv.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","bun.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","setup.mdc",".github\\setup.js",@"\.vscode\tasks.json",@"\.claude\settings.json",@"\.gemini\settings.json","folderOpen","SessionStart")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(code|cursor|claude|gemini|devenv)\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(node|bun|python(3|w)?|powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|curl|wget)\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","setup.mdc",@"\.github\setup.js",@"\.vscode\tasks.json",@"\.claude\settings.json",@"\.gemini\settings.json","folderOpen","SessionStart")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma/Hades worm's spreading phase: a Bun runtime instance making outbound HTTPS to npm publish, PyPI upload, or GitHub repo-creation/upload endpoints, indicating either token-driven package republishing or exfiltration to attacker-controlled GitHub repos as documented in the campaign writeup. Rationale: Article and corroborating writeups confirm the worm self-propagates by republishing infected packages (npm publish API, PyPI upload API) using stolen tokens, and exfiltrates harvested credentials through attacker-controlled GitHub repos. bun.exe contacting these endpoints from a developer endpoint (not a CI runner) is high-signal because developers rarely use Bun to drive npm/PyPI/GitHub APIs interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://orca.security/resources/blog/hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567 T1059.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately experimenting with Bun + npm publish for a personal package
  • Bun-based CI tool running publish in a non-CI dev environment
  • Node.js developer using a bun-runtime project that calls GitHub API for legitimate repo management
  • Renovate-bot-style tooling running under node.exe that touches api.github.com/repos
  • Engineer pushing a code snippet to a personal GitHub gist via a Bun script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Bun\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "renovate"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the bun.exe folder path (was it dropped under %TEMP%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, or a project node_modules?), pull its SHA256 and the parent process. If parent is python.exe or a folderOpen-spawned node, treat as confirmed Hades/Miasma. Step 2 — Contain: block the destination URL at the proxy/EDR network containment, isolate the device, revoke ALL of the developer's npm, PyPI, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault, and Kubernetes tokens — the article specifies these are the harvested targets. Audit GitHub for any repos created by the developer's PAT in the last 24h (worm exfil channel). Step 3 — Hunt: check the npm/PyPI registry for any package versions published by the developer's accounts in the suspect window; treat any such publication as a worm-spread event and request takedown. Run UC1, UC3, UC5 across the fleet for the same user.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun.exe","node.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish","registry.npmjs.org/-/user","upload.pypi.org/legacy","api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos","api.github.com/gists")
   or (RemoteUrl has "api.github.com" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("_index.js","bun-","setup.mjs"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish","registry.npmjs.org/-/user","upload.pypi.org/legacy","api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos","api.github.com/gists")

title: Bun Runtime Egress to npm/PyPI Publish or GitHub Repo Endpoints
id: 2f8c5a7d-9b3e-4c1f-a5d8-7e4f9b2c3d66
status: experimental
description: Detects bun.exe (or node.exe carrying the Bun payload) making outbound HTTPS to npm publish, PyPI upload, or GitHub repo/gist creation endpoints — the Miasma/Hades worm spreading and exfiltration channels.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
  dest:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'registry.npmjs.org'
      - 'upload.pypi.org'
      - 'api.github.com'
  condition: proc and dest
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe OR *\\BUN.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) @DestinationHostname:(registry.npmjs.org OR upload.pypi.org OR api.github.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(bun|node)\.exe$/i
| DomainName=/^(registry\.npmjs\.org|upload\.pypi\.org|api\.github\.com)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| count>0
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(All_Traffic.url) as urls min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe" AND (All_Traffic.url="*registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish*" OR All_Traffic.url="*registry.npmjs.org/-/user*" OR All_Traffic.url="*upload.pypi.org/legacy/*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/user/repos*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/repos/*/contents/*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/repos/*/git/refs*") by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.url) as urls min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe" AND (All_Traffic.url="*registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish*" OR All_Traffic.url="*registry.npmjs.org/-/user*" OR All_Traffic.url="*upload.pypi.org/legacy/*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/user/repos*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/repos/*/contents/*" OR All_Traffic.url="*api.github.com/repos/*/git/refs*") by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node install-time spawn downloads Bun runtime (Shai-Hulud worm pattern) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud signature where a malicious lifecycle script (preinstall/postinstall) pulls the Bun runtime mid-install to execute the stealer. The article explicitly cites Bun-runtime install during npm setup as a distinguishing behaviour of these worms. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud signature — 'installed the Bun runtime during setup'. Parent-binary set is the canonical npm/yarn/pnpm/node install chain; child predicate binds to the Bun installer URL + binary name. No legitimate package needs Bun mid-npm-install.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer genuinely migrating a project to Bun and adding it as a tooling dep
  • CI image build steps that install Bun in a Dockerfile RUN that also invokes npm in the same layer
  • Internal devx packages that install Bun as part of a polyglot toolchain setup
  • node-based shell wrappers that legitimately `npm exec bun` for repo tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker build","buildkit","buildx") and ProcessCommandLine has "bun.sh/install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree from DeviceProcessEvents around the alert — confirm `npm install` / `npm ci` was the originating command and identify the specific package whose lifecycle script kicked it off (usually visible in InitiatingProcessParentCommandLine or the working-directory node_modules path). 2) Contain: isolate the device, revoke any npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, and SSH keys that lived on it (Shai-Hulud worms exfil all three), kill the dev's session, and pin the package version in the lockfile registry-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for outbound to webhook.site / sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73 and trufflehog/secret-scanner spawns within the next 10 minutes; check GitHub audit log for new public repos created by the user's PAT in the last 24h.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","corepack.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallParents)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun install","bun run","\\bun.exe","/bun ")
   or FileName =~ "bun.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","corepack.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessName has_any (InstallParents)
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun install","bun run","\\bun.exe","/bun ")
   or ActingProcessName endswith "bun.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm/node lifecycle script downloads Bun runtime (Shai-Hulud)
id: 4b8f1c2a-7d3e-4d6a-9a1f-1e2c5b9a0d11
description: A package-manager install (npm/yarn/pnpm) or node-driven lifecycle script pulls the Bun runtime mid-install, the signature step of the Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud worms.

tags:

      - '\npm.exe'

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) @ParentImage:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\npx.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe) @CommandLine:(*bun.sh/install* OR *github.com/oven-sh/bun* OR *"bun install"* OR *"bun run"* OR *\\bun.exe*)

npm/node install-time process beaconing to webhook.site, sfrclak.com or 142.11.206.73 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the exfil-leg of the article's named campaigns where an install-time lifecycle script beacons to webhook.site (canary inbox) or to known campaign infrastructure (sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73) to ship harvested tokens. High-fidelity because legitimate npm packages do not POST credentials to webhook.site mid-install. Rationale: Hard IOCs from the article: domain sfrclak.com, IP 142.11.206.73, and webhook.site as the canary inbox commonly used by the Shai-Hulud lineage. Binding the egress to an npm/node/yarn/pnpm/bun process gates out personal webhook.site usage by developers in unrelated tooling. Sentinel query unioned across ImDnsActivity / ImNetworkSession / ImProcessCreate — no DeviceName references on tables that don't carry it.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer testing their own webhook.site inbox via a quick node REPL or `curl`-via-`npm exec` — match on InitiatingProcessParentFileName==cmd/powershell rather than npm-lifecycle parent
  • Legitimate package using webhook.site as a documented test endpoint (rare, vet by package name)
  • An internal reverse-proxy that legitimately resolves to 142.11.206.73 (verify with NetOps before suppressing)
  • Pre-existing Aikido / SafeChain telemetry callbacks if a competitor product uses webhook.site for ack
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("safe-chain","aikido") and RemoteUrl has "webhook.site")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceProcessEvents on the same DeviceId 5 minutes before the network event to identify the originating `npm install` and the specific package directory under node_modules (the script body usually drops in postinstall.js / telemetry.js / index.js of the rogue package). 2) Contain: yank network from the host, revoke npm publish tokens + GitHub PATs + cloud SSO sessions for the developer, block sfrclak.com + 142.11.206.73 at perimeter, and add the package@version to your internal denylist. 3) Hunt: tstats 30 days back for any other host that contacted those same IOCs from a node-family parent; check GitHub for new repos named like `Shai-Hulud-*` or with the user's PAT scoped to public-repo create.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","sfrclak.com"]);
let SuspectIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where RemoteUrl has_any (SuspectDomains)
   or RemoteIP in (SuspectIPs)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","sfrclak.com"]);
let SuspectIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let DnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (SuspectDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = SrcHostname, SrcIp = SrcIpAddr,
              Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "DNS";
let NetHits = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DstIpAddr in (SuspectIPs) or DstHostname has_any (SuspectDomains) or Url has_any (SuspectDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = SrcHostname, SrcIp = SrcIpAddr,
              Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url), Source = "Net";
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (InstallProcs) or ParentProcessName has_any (InstallProcs)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspectDomains) or ActingProcessCommandLine has "142.11.206.73"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = DvcHostname, SrcIp = DvcIpAddr,
              Indicator = ActingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Proc";
union DnsHits, NetHits, ProcHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Implicit node-gyp rebuild from binding.gyp spawns suspicious build child AIInstallation Medium
Targets the new attack surface the article highlights — packages without any declared scripts that still execute code via an implicit `node-gyp rebuild` triggered by binding.gyp. Detects node-gyp invoking compilers / interpreters / network tools that don't belong in a native-module build. Rationale: The article specifically names the binding.gyp / implicit `node-gyp rebuild` path as a covert execution channel that v12 will block. Genuine native-module builds spawn compilers (cl.exe, link.exe, gyp.exe) — they should never need powershell/curl/certutil. Child set is the standard LOLBin/network-downloader allowlist.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Native module that legitimately shells out to powershell to detect Windows SDK / Visual Studio paths (some node-canvas / node-sass forks)
  • node-pre-gyp using curl/wget to fetch prebuilt binaries (legitimate but article-relevant — review)
  • Developer environments running `npm install` with --verbose where parent-cmdline chaining produces false parents
  • CI nodes that wrap node-gyp in a shell script for cross-compilation
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install") and FileName =~ "curl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "github.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package owning the binding.gyp from the working directory in InitiatingProcessFolderPath (look under node_modules/<pkg>/binding.gyp), pull the SHA256 of the child binary, and dump the script body if the child is a scripting host. 2) Contain: quarantine the package version, remove from internal mirror/proxy, kick CI jobs that pulled it in the last 24h, and rotate any developer-tier secrets present in the build environment. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceFileEvents for files written under %TEMP%/%APPDATA%/.npm/_cacache during the build window, and DeviceNetworkEvents for non-prebuilt-binary URLs (anything outside github.com/<pkg> releases or the org's artifact registry).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let UnexpectedChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "binding.gyp"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "npm install"
      and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp rebuild"
| where FileName in~ (UnexpectedChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let UnexpectedChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","binding.gyp","node-gyp rebuild")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (UnexpectedChildren)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm install-time process reads .npmrc, SSH key, or cloud-credential file AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-harvesting step of Nx s1ngularity / Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud — install-time scripts read .npmrc (auth tokens), ~/.ssh/id_* (SSH keys), and AWS/GitHub credential files. The article lists these exact artefacts as what the postinstall payloads scrape. Rationale: Article enumerates exactly these victim artefacts — 'scans for tokens, SSH keys, and other goodies', and Nx s1ngularity is called out specifically as harvesting GitHub tokens, npm credentials, SSH keys, and crypto wallets. Filtering on install-time parent + ≥2 credential-file hits in one process strips out IDE indexing noise while keeping the harvester pattern.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm CLI reading user's own .npmrc during publish/login (filter on npm-cli.js parent + 'npm publish' command line)
  • VS Code remote-ssh extension's node host enumerating ~/.ssh during workspace open
  • yarn classic touching .npmrc to migrate auth tokens on first install
  • Developer running aws-sdk-node example that reads ~/.aws/credentials intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm whoami") and TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the originating process tree and the package directory under node_modules to identify the rogue package; capture the script body before the file deletes itself (article notes the harvesters self-delete). 2) Contain: immediately rotate every credential the process touched — npm tokens via `npm token revoke`, GitHub PATs in GH settings, AWS keys via IAM, force-push SSH key re-keying. Quarantine the host. 3) Hunt: search GitHub audit logs for new public repos created by the user's PAT in the last 24h (Shai-Hulud uploads stolen creds to public repos), pivot to other hosts that installed the same package@version via your internal registry logs.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([".npmrc",".ssh\\id_rsa",".ssh\\id_ed25519",".ssh\\id_ecdsa",".aws\\credentials",".config\\gh\\hosts.yml",".gitconfig",".netrc","npm\\.npmrc"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileRead","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","postinstall","preinstall")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredPaths) or FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize CredFiles = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName), 25),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count()
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
               InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where Hits >= 2 or array_length(CredFiles) >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([".npmrc",".ssh/id_rsa",".ssh/id_ed25519",".ssh/id_ecdsa",".aws/credentials",".config/gh/hosts.yml",".gitconfig",".netrc"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRead")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (InstallProcs)
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","postinstall","preinstall")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredPaths) or TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize CredFiles = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count()
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where Hits >= 2 or array_length(CredFiles) >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc

(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten) ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|npx|yarn|pnpm|bun)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\\\.npmrc|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.config\\\\gh\\\\hosts\\.yml|\\\\\\.netrc)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 1
