| tstats summariesonly=true count, dc(All_Traffic.dest) AS unique_dst_ips, dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS unique_dst_ports, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS dst_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_category!="workstation" All_Traffic.src_category!="server" (All_Traffic.src_category="iot" OR All_Traffic.src_category="printer" OR All_Traffic.src_category="camera" OR All_Traffic.src_category="router" OR All_Traffic.src_category="unknown") All_Traffic.dest_category="external" All_Traffic.transport="tcp" All_Traffic.action IN ("allowed","blocked") by All_Traffic.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where unique_dst_ips >= 200 AND unique_dst_ports <= 5 | sort - unique_dst_ips
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(All_Traffic.dest) AS unique_dst_ips, dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS unique_dst_ports, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS dst_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_category!="workstation" All_Traffic.src_category!="server" (All_Traffic.src_category="iot" OR All_Traffic.src_category="printer" OR All_Traffic.src_category="camera" OR All_Traffic.src_category="router" OR All_Traffic.src_category="unknown") All_Traffic.dest_category="external" All_Traffic.transport="tcp" All_Traffic.action IN ("allowed","blocked") by All_Traffic.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where unique_dst_ips >= 200 AND unique_dst_ports <= 5 | sort - unique_dst_ips
MIPS/MIPSel architecture-specific payload write (JDY shell-script dropper indicator) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for file writes of MIPS/MIPSel architecture binaries — uncommon outside of router/IoT firmware development. The JDY shell-script dropper specifically downloads architecture-matched payloads (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) and the article notes the binary is deleted from disk immediately after launch, so any file-event capture is high-signal. Rationale: MIPS/MIPSel naming is the article's explicit architecture token list for the JDY dropper's payload selection. On a standard corporate fleet (x86_64 Windows/Linux/macOS) these strings should not appear in file writes — the false-positive surface is essentially embedded-Linux build environments and firmware repositories, which the filter excludes. Pairs with FileOriginUrl to attribute the download source.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Embedded-Linux developer building OpenWRT / BuildRoot / Yocto images that produce MIPS toolchain output
  • Vendor firmware update download for a managed Cisco/Ubiquiti/DrayTek device
  • Security researcher / sandbox analyst staging malware samples in a lab environment
  • Backup of a router config archive labelled with its architecture
  • Git clone of a public IoT-malware repo for research purposes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/openwrt/","/buildroot/","/yocto/","/srv/build/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("make ARCH=mips","crosstool-ng","openwrt-sdk")) // exclude legitimate embedded-Linux toolchain output
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and the device role — a developer laptop running an OpenWRT build is benign; a Linux container or a quarantined IoT asset writing MIPS files to /tmp is not. Cross-reference FileOriginUrl/FileOriginIP against threat intel and check whether the source IP appears in any UC1 cohort. 2) Contain: if non-developer asset, isolate immediately, preserve the file (the article notes self-deletion, so racing to copy it matters) and capture memory if the process is still resident. Block the download URL at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the FileOriginIP across the last 30 days for any other internal asset that downloaded from the same source, look for child processes of the dropper that match wget/curl + chmod + execute patterns typical of shell-script droppers, and feed the FileOriginIP back into UC3 to check whether the host began scanning shortly after.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-]|$)"
   or FileOriginUrl matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-/?]|$)"
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/firmware","/var/lib/firmware","/opt/openwrt","buildroot"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
imFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\._\-])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-]|$)"
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("openwrt","buildroot","yocto"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MIPS Architecture Binary Written to Disk Indicating IoT/SOHO Botnet Dropper
id: c1f4e3a2-8b6d-4e1f-9c2a-7d3b8e5a1c4f
description: Detects creation of files whose name carries a MIPS/MIPSel architecture token (mips, mipsel, mips64, mipsel64). The JDY botnet's shell-script dropper downloads architecture-matched payloads to recruit edge devices and self-deletes the binary after launch, so file-create capture is high-signal.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|re|i: '(^|.*[\._\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\._\-/]|$)'
  filter_buildtools:
    Image|contains:
      - '/openwrt/'
      - '/buildroot/'
      - '/yocto/'
  condition: selection and not filter_buildtools
level: medium

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH (@file.path:*mips* OR @file.path:*mipsel* OR @file.path:*mips64* OR @file.path:*mipsel64*) -@process.executable.path:/openwrt/* -@process.executable.path:/buildroot/*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)(^|[\\._\\-/])(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)([\\._\\-/]|$)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/openwrt/i OR ContextImageFileName=/buildroot/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Filesystem.file_path) AS paths, values(Filesystem.process_name) AS writers from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" (Filesystem.file_name="*.mips" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mips64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mips_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mipsel_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mips-*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mipsel-*") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_name, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=left dest [ search index=web earliest=-1h (uri_path="*mips*" OR uri_path="*mipsel*") | stats values(url) AS download_url values(src) AS download_src by dest ] | table _time, dest, user, file_name, paths, writers, download_url
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.file_path) AS paths, values(Filesystem.process_name) AS writers from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" (Filesystem.file_name="*.mips" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mips64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.mipsel64" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mips_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*mipsel_*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mips-*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*-mipsel-*") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_name, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=left dest [ search index=web earliest=-1h (uri_path="*mips*" OR uri_path="*mipsel*") | stats values(url) AS download_url values(src) AS download_src by dest ] | table _time, dest, user, file_name, paths, writers, download_url

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)

    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 exploit attempt via /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) MICS configuration endpoint that watchTowr Labs disclosed as the vulnerable path for CVE-2026-10520 unauthenticated OS command injection. Any request to this URI on a Sentry appliance after the 2026-06-09 patch is high-fidelity for exploit attempts, since the patched code redirects unauthenticated requests to the login page. Rationale: Endpoint string `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` and backend handler `handleExecute()` are the exact strings disclosed by watchTowr Labs and quoted verbatim in the article. Corroborated by watchTowr's labs.watchtowr.com writeup, Rapid7 ETR blog, eSentire advisory, and the watchtowrlabs GitHub PoC; Shadowserver observed at least 19 vulnerable instances being probed and 2 already backdoored, so a hit on this URI is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://www.esentire.com/security-advisories/critical-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/ • https://github.com/watchtowrlabs/watchTowr-vs-Ivanti-Sentry-RCE-CVE-2026-10520-CVE-2026-10523
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing the Sentry asset with authenticated credentials
  • watchTowr detection artefact generator run by an internal red/purple team to verify patch status
  • Ivanti support diagnostic check from an authenticated MICS session
  • Misconfigured monitoring agent fetching the configuration endpoint as a health-check
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("<qualys-scanner-ip>", "<tenable-scanner-ip>", "<internal-redteam-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on SourceIP and check whether the request returned 200/302/500 — a 302 to the login page indicates the patch is in place and the attempt failed; a 200 on an unpatched build indicates likely successful injection. Pull a sample request body (CEF RequestContext / IIS query string) and grep for shell-metacharacters (`;`, `|`, backticks, `$(`). 2) Contain: if the Sentry version is below R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1, isolate the appliance from the internet immediately and snapshot it; assume root-level compromise per Shadowserver telemetry. Rotate admin credentials and ActiveSync/MDM enrolment tokens that traverse Sentry. 3) Hunt: review the appliance for new local accounts, modified `/etc/passwd`, fresh cron entries, listening sockets on non-standard ports, and outbound connections from the Sentry's IP to non-Ivanti destinations over the past 14 days. Cross-check Defender / Sentinel for downstream lateral movement from the Sentry host's IP.

)

title: Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 Exploitation Attempt (handleMessage endpoint)
id: 9c0b9d2a-3e1f-4d8b-9f02-7a8b6c1d4e95
description: Detects HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry MICS configuration endpoint /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage disclosed by watchTowr Labs as the sink for CVE-2026-10520 unauthenticated OS command injection that yields root-level RCE. After the 2026-06-09 patch, unauthenticated requests to this path are redirected to the login page, so any direct hit on patched instances or any hit on unpatched instances is high-fidelity exploit activity.
references:
  - https://labs.watchtowr.com/more-evidence-that-words-dont-mean-what-we-thought-they-meant-ivanti-sentry-pre-auth-os-command-injection-cve-2026-10520/

Devices running unpatched Ivanti Sentry / FortiSandbox / SAP NetWeaver versions (June 2026 advisory) AIReconnaissance High
Inventories assets whose installed software version is in the affected range published in the 2026-06-09/10 Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP advisories. Surfaces the exposure window between patch release and rollout for the seven critical CVEs the article enumerates so the SOC can prioritise the network-facing Ivanti Sentry and FortiSandbox boxes first. Rationale: CVE list and affected versions (FortiSandbox 5.0.0-5.0.5 / 4.4.0-4.4.8; Ivanti Sentry pre-R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1; SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP, Commerce Cloud, Data Hub, Java Web Container) are quoted directly from the article. The Defender TVM and Splunk Vulnerabilities DM both key on CveId so the query is exact, not regex; joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the network-facing Ivanti Sentry / FortiSandbox appliances first. Corroborated by Rapid7 ETR and Help Net Security advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523-multiple-critical-vulnerabilities-affecting-ivanti-sentry/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/10/ivanti-sentry-cve-2026-10520-cve-2026-10523/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Device shown as vulnerable because the TVM scan ran before the patch installation finished — re-scan after maintenance window closes
  • SAP test/sandbox instance intentionally pinned to an old version for regression testing
  • FortiSandbox box being decommissioned and excluded from patching by an approved change ticket
  • Devices with stale agent check-ins reporting last-known version that has since been upgraded
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort the result by IsInternetFacing=true first — Ivanti Sentry and FortiSandbox boxes exposed to the public PoC chain are the immediate fire. Cross-reference each DeviceName with the CMDB to confirm it's actually a production appliance not a lab snapshot. 2) Contain: for internet-facing vulnerable Ivanti Sentry, apply the upstream WAF rule blocking `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` until the device is upgraded; for FortiSandbox WEB UI, restrict management-plane access to the admin VLAN. Open a P1 patch ticket per host with the RecommendedSecurityUpdate value. 3) Hunt: pair this list with the companion UC1 detection — for every device listed here, retro-hunt 30 days of WAF / CommonSecurityLog for requests to the handleMessage endpoint and for SAP NetWeaver hosts retro-hunt for anomalous SAML responses and crafted RFC traffic targeting CVE-2026-44748 / CVE-2026-27671.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-25089", "CVE-2026-10520", "CVE-2026-10523", "CVE-2026-44748", "CVE-2026-27671", "CVE-2026-22732", "CVE-2026-40128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] CISA KEV June 2026 - Vulnerable Cisco SD-WAN / Chrome / Arista assets in inventory · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Arista EOS CVE-2026-7473 - Unexpected Tunneled Traffic to Configured VTEP / GRE · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Chrome V8 CVE-2026-11645 - Suspicious non-browser child of chrome.exe (renderer escape) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Arista EOS CVE-2026-7473 - Unexpected Tunneled Traffic to Configured VTEP / GRE AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for VXLAN (UDP/4789) or GRE traffic reaching an Arista 7020R/7280R/7500R VTEP from sources outside the legitimate overlay fabric. Per Arista's advisory the switch decapsulates any tunnel whose outer destination matches the configured decap IP regardless of inner protocol, so any unexpected source contacting the VTEP is a potential exploitation attempt of CVE-2026-7473. Rationale: Arista's published mitigation explicitly names VXLAN (UDP/4789) and GRE as the abusable encapsulations and 7020R/7280R/R2/7500R/R2 as the impacted platforms. Detection pivots on tunnel-destined traffic from non-RFC1918 sources and on EOS syslog where the agent reports the unexpected decap path. Cross-checked against Arista's advisory phrasing in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate eVPN/VXLAN peering from a partner ASN whose source range was never added to the IPAM lookup
  • Network engineer testing GRE tunnel from a jump host on a public-IP allocation
  • Cloud-burst overlay where the remote VTEP genuinely lives on a public address (Azure VWAN, AWS Transit Gateway Connect)
  • Monitoring probe (NetSnmp, BFD reflector) issuing VXLAN-encapsulated keepalives
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP in (toscalar(externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://internal-ipam/known_partner_vteps.csv"] with(format="csv"))))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: confirm the destination IP is actually a configured VTEP / GRE endpoint per Arista's advisory list (7020R/7280R/7500R series only); pull the matching EOS flow record and verify the inner protocol is something the overlay should NOT carry. Step 2 — contain: apply the upstream-ACL mitigation Arista recommends — `permit udp <legit-source-block> any eq 4789` then `deny udp any any eq 4789` on the L3 transit interface, plus equivalent GRE filter. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on the source IP across NetFlow for the last 30 days; look for prior reconnaissance (port scans, ICMP probing) and any internal hosts that received decapsulated traffic post-decap.
let arista_hosts = dynamic(["arista","eos","vtep"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HostName has_any (arista_hosts) or Computer has_any (arista_hosts)
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(VXLAN|GRE|decap|tunnel)"
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(unexpected|invalid|mismatch|drop|denied|non-configured)"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=HostName, EvSource="syslog", DestinationPort=int(null), SourceAddr="", DestAddr="", AppProto="", Detail=SyslogMessage
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DeviceVendor =~ "Arista" or DeviceProduct has "EOS"
  | where DestinationPort == 4789 or ApplicationProtocol has_any ("vxlan","gre")
  | where not(SourceIP startswith "10.") and not(SourceIP startswith "192.168.") and not(SourceIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DeviceExternalID, EvSource="cef", DestinationPort, SourceAddr=SourceIP, DestAddr=DestinationIP, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol, Detail=Message
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:*arista* OR @host.name:*vtep* OR @syslog.appname:*Tunnel* OR @syslog.appname:*Decap*) (@syslog.message:*VXLAN* OR @syslog.message:*GRE* OR @syslog.message:*tunnel*) (@syslog.message:*unexpected* OR @syslog.message:*invalid* OR @syslog.message:*mismatch* OR @syslog.message:*non-configured*)

Chrome V8 CVE-2026-11645 - Suspicious non-browser child of chrome.exe (renderer escape) AIExploitation High
V8 OOB read/write inside the renderer sandbox typically chains to a sandbox escape that spawns a non-browser child process. This UC catches chrome.exe / msedge.exe / brave.exe spawning LOLBins or shells immediately after a drive-by visit, which is the post-exploitation pivot for CVE-2026-11645. Rationale: Article confirms CVE-2026-11645 is a V8 OOB read/write actively exploited via crafted HTML — the canonical exploitation tail is a non-browser child of chrome.exe. Chrome's own utility/renderer processes always carry --type= / --utility-sub-type= flags, which we exclude to keep the FP rate near zero. Article cross-referenced with CVE summary on KEV catalog (added 2026-06-10). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/
ATT&CKT1203 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM/EDR agent invoking certutil via a browser-initiated install flow
  • Developer running `chrome.exe --no-sandbox` and chain-launching cmd from devtools-integration extensions
  • Selenium / Playwright test harness driving chromium with custom subprocess hooks
  • Enterprise PKI enrolment pages that legitimately spawn certutil to install a user cert
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--no-sandbox","--headless") or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Google LLC","Microsoft Corporation","Brave Software Inc."))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull the browser version from `InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion` and check it against the Chrome stable release that ships the CVE-2026-11645 fix; pull the parent browser's URL history for the 60s before the child spawn. Step 2 — contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, revoke the user's primary refresh token in Entra ID, force a Chrome auto-update. Step 3 — hunt: 30-day sweep on DeviceNetworkEvents for the device contacting any IP the child process reached out to, plus a tenant-wide search for the same parent-child shape over the last 24h to catch other victims of the same exploit kit.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--type=","--utility-sub-type=","--enable-features="))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          BrowserVersion = InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let chromium = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe"]);
let lolbins = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe"]);
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentLeaf = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| extend ChildLeaf  = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ParentLeaf in (chromium)

| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("--type=","--utility-sub-type=","--enable-features="))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV June 2026 - Vulnerable Cisco SD-WAN / Chrome / Arista assets in inventory AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces every device in the estate still exposed to CVE-2026-20245 (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager), CVE-2026-11645 (Chrome V8) or CVE-2026-7473 (Arista EOS) — the three CVEs CISA added to KEV on 2026-06-10 with an FCEB remediation deadline of 2026-06-23. Drives patch prioritisation rather than chasing post-compromise tells. Rationale: Article lists the three KEV-added CVEs with their CVSS scores and the FCEB June-23 deadline verbatim. A KEV-exposure hunting rule is the highest-leverage detection a SOC can ship against an article whose primary message is 'patch by date X'. No external corroboration needed beyond the KEV catalog itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioned hosts still reporting via Defender that have since been retired
  • Lab/testbed Arista 7280R intentionally kept on an old EOS build
  • Pre-prod Chrome builds (Beta/Canary) where the vulnerable version is expected
  • SD-WAN appliance flagged but isolated on a management VLAN with no inbound exposure
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: rank exposed hosts by internet-facing role (DMZ Arista VTEPs > SD-WAN Manager > end-user Chrome installs); cross-reference with DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing where available. Step 2 — contain: for Arista, apply the upstream-ACL mitigation Arista published (no patch is planned); for Chrome, push the auto-update channel; for Cisco SD-WAN Manager, apply Cisco PSIRT's patch. Step 3 — hunt: parallel-launch the Chrome-child and Arista-tunnel UCs above against the exposed-asset list; check Defender alert history (last 14d) for any AlertEvidence already touching these hosts.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Web-facing exposure of dev.env / .env config file (returns 200) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts HTTP requests to dev.env / .env / .env.* paths that returned a 2xx response, indicating a misconfigured web server is leaking the very file that ships AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random. CVE-2026-48031 weaponises exactly this file, so any successful retrieval is a direct precursor to JWT forgery. Rationale: Targets the exact filename (dev.env) named at line 10 of the advisory plus common .env variants the same template is renamed to. 2xx/3xx status confirms the leak actually happened. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory and dhax/go-base PR #31. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline pulling .env from a private artifact server
  • DAST/SAST scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nessus) probing for exposed dotfiles
  • Penetration testers running ffuf / dirsearch with default wordlists
  • Internal developer documentation site serving a sanitized .env.example
  • Cloud config-management agents (Consul, etcd) syncing env templates over HTTP
Suppression filter
and csUserAgent !has_any ("Burp","OWASP ZAP","Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","ffuf","dirsearch","gobuster") and cIP !in (KnownScannerIPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on cIP/sourceIPAddress; was the request from a known scanner, a developer subnet, or external? Inspect User-Agent and response size — non-empty 200 on dev.env is critical. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET immediately to a 32+ byte random value, invalidate all outstanding JWT/refresh tokens, and add a WebACL/NGINX deny for .env/dev.env paths. Take the affected service off the perimeter if the secret was leaked externally. 3) Hunt: look for forged-token use — admin API calls from the same source IP within 24h, /api/v1/token/refresh hits with unknown sub claims, and any new sessions whose iat predates the secret rotation. Sweep all Go services for github.com/dhax/go-base in go.mod.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/dev.env","/.env","/.env.dev","/.env.local","/.env.development")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe","goland64.exe","idea64.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// IIS-fronted Go service exposure
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$"
| where scStatus in (200,206,301,302)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| union (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DeviceProduct in ("WAF","Application Gateway","CloudFront","NGINX","Apache")
    | where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)(\?|$)"
    | where toint(EventOutcome) between (200 .. 399)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, sSiteName=DestinationHostName, cIP=SourceIP, csMethod=RequestMethod, csUriStem=RequestURL, csUriQuery="", scStatus=toint(EventOutcome), csUserAgent=RequestClientApplication
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web exposure of dev.env / .env config file
id: 7c1a4b3e-2f57-4c61-9c4e-3a1e2f8b5d11
description: Detects HTTP requests retrieving dev.env or .env files that may leak the hardcoded AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random used by github.com/dhax/go-base (CVE-2026-48031).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
  - https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.reconnaissance
  - attack.t1592.002
  - attack.t1083
  - cve.2026.48031
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|re|i: '(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$'
  selection_status:
    sc-status:
      - 200
      - 206
      - 301
      - 302
  condition: selection_path and selection_status
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:cloudfront OR source:caddy) @http.url_details.path:(*/dev.env OR */.env OR */.env.dev OR */.env.local OR */.env.development) @http.status_code:[200 TO 399]
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ConnectionDirection=1
| (RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=3000 OR RemotePort=8080)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest | DomainName=/.*/ }, field=[aid], include=[DomainName])
| regex("/(dev\.env|\.env)(\.[a-z]+)?($|\?)", field=CommandLine, strict=false)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail/dataevents (S3 object-level events)
fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.bucketName, requestParameters.key, errorCode
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["GetObject", "GetObjectAcl"]
      and (requestParameters.key like /(?i)(^|\/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$/)
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

github.com/dhax/go-base supply-chain footprint in go.mod / build artifacts AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts (developer laptops, CI runners, container build agents) where go.mod, go.sum, vendor/modules.txt or Dockerfiles reference github.com/dhax/go-base. The advisory states 'all versions before commit cc82b974...' are vulnerable, so footprinting the dependency is the first step before patching can begin. Rationale: Anchors on the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base named in the advisory's Affected Component list. go.mod / go.sum / Dockerfile additions and `go build`/`go mod` invocations that reference the module pin the asset surface that needs patching to the cc82b974... commit. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/commits/master
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1518
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer evaluating the boilerplate for a new microservice
  • Security team running SCA scan that already covers this CVE
  • CI job intentionally pinning to the patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6)
  • Internal fork of go-base that is already patched
  • Vulnerability scanner (Trivy, Grype, Snyk) reading go.sum files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trivy.exe","grype.exe","snyk.exe","syft.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every host/build agent that touched go.mod referencing dhax/go-base in the last 30d. For each, pull the pinned version (the @ pseudo-version after the path). Anything before commit cc82b9740fa6 (2026-05-17) is vulnerable. 2) Contain: file Jira/Linear tickets to bump the dependency past cc82b9740fa6, regenerate AUTH_JWT_SECRET (>=32 chars), and force a token revocation on next deploy. Block new builds on the unpatched version via a renovate/dependabot policy. 3) Hunt: identify all running services derived from the vulnerable code — query container registries for images whose go.mod includes the unpatched pin. For any that were ever internet-facing, run the JWT-forgery UC against their access logs back to the deploy date.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("go.mod","go.sum","modules.txt","Dockerfile")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| union (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
       or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType="ProcessCmdline", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine
)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("go.mod","go.sum","modules.txt","Dockerfile")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has "dhax/go-base"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath=ActingProcessName, TargetFileName=ActingProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Admin / privileged API call without a preceding SUCCESSFUL login (JWT forgery indicator) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Forged tokens signed with the hardcoded 'random' secret never traverse the application's login or refresh flows — they appear as bearer-auth-only requests. This UC pivots web access logs for /api/v1/admin/* and /api/v1/me hits whose source IP has no /api/v1/login/* 2xx in the prior 24h, the behavioural signature of token forgery. Rationale: The advisory's PoC explicitly hits /api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, and /api/v1/token/refresh with a forged Bearer token (no login step). Modelling 'admin hit without a recent successful login from same IP' captures that footprint without requiring the JWT to be parsed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Long-lived legitimate session whose original login was >24h ago (refresh token kept it alive)
  • Service-to-service auth using a static API key rather than the login flow
  • Healthcheck / synthetic monitoring hitting /api/v1/me with a pre-baked token
  • CI smoke tests that obtain tokens out of band and never use /login
  • NAT'd corporate egress where many users share one source IP and not all have logged in
Suppression filter
and csUserName !in ("healthcheck","synthetics","datadog","newrelic") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","Datadog Synthetics","kube-probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JWT from the Authorization header — decode header+payload (no signature check needed) and verify the 'sub' and 'roles' claims match a real user. Compare 'iat' against the user's last legitimate login from your IdP. 2) Contain: if the token is forged, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32+ byte random value, restart the Go service, and force-revoke all sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull all requests from the same IP and from the same user-agent over the prior 30 days. Look for /api/v1/admin/users enumeration, mass /api/v1/me lookups across different sub claims (token re-use across identities), and any state-changing POST/PUT/DELETE that may have already exfiltrated data.
let AdminHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)

    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl;
let LoginHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(48h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/login/","/api/v1/auth/")
    | summarize LastLogin = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on RemoteIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', Timestamp, LastLogin) > 24
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LastLogin, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)

let LoginHits = W3CIISLog

Internal host clones / curls github.com/dhax/go-base or raw dev.env AIReconnaissance Medium
Catches developer or attacker hosts pulling the vulnerable boilerplate — either via 'git clone github.com/dhax/go-base', 'go get', or direct curl/wget of raw.githubusercontent.com/dhax/go-base/.../dev.env. Either action seeds the secret 'random' onto a system that may later run the service or be used to forge tokens. Rationale: Hits the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base from the advisory's Affected Component plus the raw.githubusercontent.com pattern used when an attacker just wants the leaked dev.env without cloning. Narrowing to git/go/curl/wget keeps the volume sane. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base
ATT&CKT1593.003 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer learning Go and trying the popular boilerplate (1,685 stars on GitHub)
  • Security researcher pulling the repo to reproduce the CVE
  • CI mirror sync that mirrors many public Go modules including go-base
  • Internal training material that references go-base as an example
  • Dependency-resolution side-effect when a transitive module points back here
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("renovate","dependabot","snyk.exe","trivy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the host — is it a dev workstation, a build agent, or a production server? Production server is the worst case. Capture the destination path of the clone to know where the secret 'random' now lives on disk. 2) Contain: if production, rip out the deployed artifact and rebuild from a patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6). On dev hosts, ensure the dev.env file is not later copied into a release container. 3) Hunt: from the same host/user, look for subsequent 'go build' artifacts being pushed to internal registries, container image pushes labelled with the developer's name, and any web service deployed from those artifacts now serving /api/v1/* on the network.

JWT token in HTTP Authorization header verifying against secret 'random' AIActions on Objectives High
Decodes Bearer JWTs from web access logs and verifies their HMAC-SHA256 signature against the literal key 'random'. A successful verification is a smoking-gun forged token from the public CVE-2026-48031 secret. This is the highest-confidence detection but requires a custom enrichment step in the SIEM ingestion pipeline. Rationale: Implements the article's exact PoC inversely — the attacker uses 'random' as the HMAC key to sign; we use it to verify. Any token that verifies with key='random' is, by definition, a forged token because patched versions log.Fatal on that secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester actively exploiting the CVE during an authorised engagement
  • Pre-prod environment that still ships the unpatched dev.env intentionally for testing
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting a PoC against the production endpoint
  • An unrelated service that coincidentally also uses HS256 with the (weak) key 'random' for a different purpose
  • Token-replay testing tools (e.g. Burp JWT extension) being run by red team
Suppression filter
and SourceIP !in (KnownPenTesterIPs) and not (Environment == "staging" and ServiceName startswith "goose-base-test-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the affected endpoint is running github.com/dhax/go-base. Decode the JWT 'sub' and 'roles' claims and check whether they correspond to a real user or a fabricated identity. Any 'roles' containing 'admin' is automatic priority-1. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to `openssl rand -base64 32`, redeploy the service to invalidate all outstanding tokens, force-logout all users, then patch the dhax/go-base dependency past commit cc82b9740fa6. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull every request from the offending IP over 30d; cross-correlate with DB audit logs for /api/v1/admin/users access, profile reads (/api/v1/me), and any state-mutating POST/PUT/DELETE. Identify what was touched and prepare a breach-notification scope.

| where Forged == "true"
| extend JWTSubject = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTSubject)
| extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTRoles)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

    | extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTRoles)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, RequestClientApplication;
Forged
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
Domainso4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON · [LLM] build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering 1.4.1 build.rs harvesting host repo metadata by spawning `git log -n 1 --pretty=format:{"commit":"%H","author":"%an",...}` from a Cargo build-script process. The JSON pretty-format template plus a Cargo build-script parent is the article-specific fingerprint of the exfil step. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim --pretty=format JSON template strings the article shows in the build.rs payload (`commit`, `%H`, `author`, `%an`, `email`, `%ae`) combined with a Cargo build-script parent (rustc compiles build.rs to a binary named `build-script-build` on Windows/Linux). Routine `git log` calls from IDEs/CI don't carry this exact JSON tag set parented by a build-script process. Cross-checked the build-script-build naming via the official Cargo build-script reference (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html) and the upstream maintainer issue https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1005 T1195.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer tooling (rust-analyzer, IDE git extensions) running git log with --pretty=format but using a CSV/tab template, not the JSON tag set above
  • CI scripts running git log --pretty=format from a shell, not parented by build-script-build
  • Custom internal Rust crates whose legitimate build.rs invokes git for version-stamping (usually only `git rev-parse HEAD`, not multi-field JSON metadata)
  • Cargo workspace tooling like `cargo-edit` or `cargo-release` shelling out to git from rustc context
  • Manual test of the cenotelie/onering repository itself by a researcher reproducing the IOC
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("%H", "%an", "%ae")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture full process tree (cargo→rustc→build-script-build→git), the Cargo.lock and Cargo.toml on the host, and the user's home repo path; confirm `onering` 1.4.1 is in the dependency graph (`cargo tree | grep onering`). 2) Contain: isolate the dev workstation from the network, kill the cargo build, revoke any source-control PATs the user has cached (gh, git credential-manager), and force-push-protect any branches the user touched in the last 24h. 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId reaching o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io or any /api/4511539669368912/envelope/ POST in the last 30 days, pivot on every other host that resolved that domain, and search Cargo.lock files repo-wide for `onering` at v1.4.1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an", "email", "%ae")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering build.rs exfiltration POST: curl invoked with the specific Sentry envelope URL (project id 4511539669368912 / org id o4511539639222272) and the `application/x-sentry-envelope` Content-Type, parented by a Cargo build-script process. This is the network-layer half of the exfil chain. Rationale: Article gives the verbatim Sentry ingest URL, DSN public key, organization id and project id. Curl parented by a Cargo build-script with any of those four strings in the cmdline is essentially deterministic for the onering payload. The combination forecloses noise from legit Sentry users (none would have curl invoked by build-script-build) and from legit Cargo builds (none would POST to a Sentry envelope). Cross-checked the Sentry envelope endpoint format at docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/ • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using Sentry crash-reporting from Rust code, but invoked via the sentry-rust SDK at runtime (not via curl in a build script)
  • Developer manually testing the IOC for IR/research purposes from the same host
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem mirror where the URL happens to contain the same project id substring
  • Penetration-test simulation of supply-chain exfil using these exact IOCs
  • Threat-intel platform crawler fetching the article URL into a curl trace logged by EDR
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the curl process tree, extract the POST body if proxy/PCAP available, and confirm the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821 in the URL path. Pull Cargo.lock on the host and grep for `onering`. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the cargo build, block o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io at the proxy, rotate any source-tree secrets the recent commit may have touched (treat the recent diff as exposed). 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the destination domain across the fleet for the last 30 days; pivot on every internal repo whose Cargo.lock contains onering 1.4.1; alert affected dev leads that recent commits leaked.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "curl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/curl"
| where CommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("build-script-build", "build_script_build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path AICommand & Control High
Wire-side catch-all for hosts reaching the article's Sentry ingest domain or the project-specific `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/` path — independent of the process that initiated it (covers proxied/wrapped variants and Linux/macOS dev hosts where Cargo runs). Rationale: Article names the exact ingest hostname `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` and project envelope path `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/`. Domain alone is so specific that any internal DNS resolution or HTTP request to it is high-confidence — and catches process variants (the maintainer's GitHub repo is also compromised, so the payload could land via `git clone` rather than crates.io). 30-day lookback because exfil-per-commit means even one historical hit is interesting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using a Sentry org with the same numeric org-id (collisions are astronomically unlikely for this specific id but technically possible)
  • Threat-intel platform proxy fetching the article or IOC bundles citing the domain
  • Detection-engineering lab host reproducing the IOC for rule tuning
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem instance whose path namespace happens to coincide (won't share the public DNS name)
  • Browser preview from analyst clicking the article URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich the source host with cargo / Rust toolchain inventory and recent process tree; identify the process that owned the egress (curl vs sentry-rust SDK vs something else). 2) Contain: sinkhole `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at corporate DNS and add a deny on the URL path at the egress proxy; isolate impacted hosts; treat the most recent git diff on each impacted repo as leaked and rotate any secrets it touched. 3) Hunt: dump every host that resolved the domain in the last 90 days; for each, run `cargo tree` against every repo on disk for `onering` 1.4.1; check the maintainer's GitHub repo (https://github.com/cenotelie/onering) is pinned to a vetted commit, not main.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where AdditionalFields has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or Url has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName),
