 | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1 AIDelivery Medium
Catches the supply-chain ingress: file writes to Cargo.lock / Cargo.toml mentioning the malicious crate version, or HTTPS downloads of the onering 1.4.1 crate tarball from crates.io. Targets the build-time moment when a dev pulls the poisoned dependency, before build.rs runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit IOC `onering 1.4.1 from crates.io`. Cargo writes the cache file `onering-1.4.1.crate` under `~/.cargo/registry/cache/<index>/` and updates Cargo.lock with the pinned version on resolve — both are deterministic side-effects of pulling the poisoned dep. Article also flags that the GitHub repo is compromised, so we keep the file-write detection generic enough to fire on git-cloned dependencies (where the URL fetch wouldn't trigger). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or detection engineer intentionally fetching the IOC for sandboxing
  • Mirror/proxy of crates.io pre-fetching the malicious version into local cache before a yank propagates
  • Vulnerability scanner like cargo-audit or Aikido enumerating the version
  • Legacy CI pipeline still referencing onering 1.4.1 after yank but on an isolated build agent
  • Developer cleaning up `Cargo.lock` after a known-bad pull (Cargo writes the file even on `cargo update --precise` to a safe version, with onering removed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the host's `~/.cargo/registry/cache/**/onering-1.4.1.crate` and confirm SHA256 matches the malicious tarball; grep every repo on disk for `onering` in Cargo.lock and note the version. 2) Contain: instruct the dev to `cargo update -p onering --precise <safe-version>` or remove the dependency, force a fresh `cargo build` in a clean target dir, and on shared CI invalidate the cargo cache. 3) Hunt: across the org's source-control, run `git grep -E 'onering.*=.*"1\.4\.1"'` on every Rust repo; check internal Cargo mirrors for any hosts that pulled the bad version; coordinate with Aikido feed for org-wide blast radius.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "crates.io" and (RemoteUrl has "onering/1.4.1" or RemoteUrl has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cargo.exe", "cargo")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FolderPath has ".cargo\\registry\\cache" or FolderPath has ".cargo/registry/cache"
 | where FileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Url has "crates.io" and (Url has "onering/1.4.1" or Url has "onering-1.4.1.crate")
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName in~ ("Cargo.lock", "Cargo.toml")
 | where ActingProcessName has "cargo"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where TargetFileName has "onering-1.4.1"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:zeek (@http.url:*crates.io*onering\/1.4.1* OR @http.url:*crates.io*onering-1.4.1.crate*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:*\/.cargo\/registry\/cache\/*onering-1.4.1*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\.cargo\\registry\\cache\\*onering-1.4.1* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Cargo.lock OR @TargetFilename:*\\Cargo.toml))
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/onering-1\.4\.1/i OR (TargetFileName=/[\\/](Cargo\.lock|Cargo\.toml)$/i ContextImageFileName=/cargo(\.exe)?$/i))) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(static\.)?crates\.io/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Unpatched June 2026 critical Microsoft CVEs — inventory & exposure pivot AIWeaponization High
Hunts for endpoints still missing the June 2026 Patch Tuesday updates that address the article-named critical RCE/SFB/EoP CVEs (CVE-2026-45657 kernel UAF, -47291 HTTP.sys, -44815 DHCP, -45586 CTFMON, -49160 HTTP/2 Bomb, -50507/45585 BitLocker). Pivots TVM data against DeviceInfo so internet-facing or DHCP-serving hosts surface first. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs disclosed in the June 2026 Microsoft advisory bulletin so the hit-list is article-specific rather than a generic 'critical CVE' query; joining DeviceInfo prioritises IsInternetFacing hosts which matches the pre-auth network-RCE risk profile of CVE-2026-45657/47291/44815.
ATT&CKT1190 T1588.006
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities Endpoint.Computer_Inventory
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices that patched but haven't re-reported TVM telemetry within 24h
  • Out-of-band patched (e.g. preview channel) machines still showing legacy KB
  • VDI golden images marked vulnerable but clones already patched
  • Servers under maintenance windows scheduled for next cycle
Suppression filter
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)  // exclude stale TVM rows
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is genuinely missing the June 2026 cumulative update via WMI Win32_QuickFixEngineering or `wmic qfe list | findstr KB` rather than trusting TVM lag. 2) Contain: for internet-facing or DHCP-serving hosts, block inbound 67/68 (DHCP), 80/443 (HTTP.sys) and TCP/IP exposure via NSG/firewall until patched; force an emergency patch ring. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'RoguePlanet' and 'DHCP svchost anomalous child' on the same DeviceId for the past 30d to detect any exploitation that may have already occurred pre-patch.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP

RoguePlanet PoC — cmd/powershell spawned by MsMpEng.exe with SYSTEM integrity AIExploitation High
Catches Chaotic Eclipse's RoguePlanet race-condition exploit which spawns a SYSTEM command prompt from the Microsoft Defender service process (MsMpEng.exe). MsMpEng.exe spawning an interactive shell at SYSTEM integrity is a hard zero-baseline behaviour — Defender never legitimately launches cmd/powershell. Rationale: Article explicitly names RoguePlanet as 'a race condition that could be used to spawn a Windows command prompt with SYSTEM privileges' against Defender — MsMpEng.exe (the Defender AM service) as parent of cmd/powershell is the exact behavioural fingerprint and has zero legitimate baseline.
ATT&CKT1068 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender platform update install paths that briefly invoke a helper shell (rare, version-specific)
  • Microsoft engineering MDM dump/repair scripts run via support
  • Custom EDR/SOAR playbook injecting a diagnostic command through MpCmdRun.exe (parent would actually be MpCmdRun, not MsMpEng — should not match)
  • Lab/sandbox VMs running offensive-security training PoCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Platform\\" or ProcessCommandLine !has "MpDiag"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree (MsMpEng.exe → cmd → grandchildren) and the SHA256 of any grandchild; check if the host already had June 2026 patches per UC1. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender 'Isolate machine' action and reset the logged-on user's credentials — SYSTEM shell means full host compromise. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents for any process with InitiatingProcessFileName=MsMpEng.exe across the fleet for the last 30 days; also check DeviceFileEvents for files written by MsMpEng.exe outside %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Windows Defender.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in~ ("System","High")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\MsMpEng.exe"
| extend NewProc = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewProc in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where TokenElevationType in ("%%1936","%%1937")  // Type1 full / Type2 elevated
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
title: RoguePlanet PoC - Shell Spawned by Microsoft Defender MsMpEng.exe
id: f4d2a1b7-83e6-4c19-9c5d-a7b3e2f1c0d8
description: Detects cmd.exe/powershell.exe spawned by MsMpEng.exe (Microsoft Defender Antimalware Service), behaviour aligned with Chaotic Eclipse's RoguePlanet race-condition PoC granting SYSTEM-level shell.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-patches-record-206-flaws.html

    Image|endswith:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\MsMpEng.exe OR *\msmpeng.exe OR *\MSMPENG.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\PWSH.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/MsMpEng\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, IntegrityLevel], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","conhost.exe") AND Processes.process_integrity_level="system" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="MsMpEng.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","conhost.exe") AND Processes.process_integrity_level="system" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
CVE-2026-44815 DHCP Client RCE — anomalous child of svchost hosting Dhcp service AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the Windows DHCP Client service host (svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -s Dhcp) spawning any process other than its narrow legitimate set. CVE-2026-44815 is a pre-auth stack overflow in dhcpcsvc giving code execution inside that svchost — successful exploitation surfaces as a child process originating from the DHCP svchost instance. Rationale: Article quotes Action1's analysis that CVE-2026-44815 'turns network traffic into a full system compromise' via DHCP services — the DHCP Client runs inside a specific svchost instance (-s Dhcp, NetworkService account); any non-WerFault child of that exact svchost is post-exploitation execution. Excluding DhcpServer disambiguates from the separate Server service host.
ATT&CKT1190 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft cumulative update post-install spawning dpkginst-style helpers that briefly attach to svchost children
  • Third-party NAC agents (ForeScout, Cisco ISE) that hook DHCP for posture checks
  • Sysinternals/procmon traces capturing svchost trees during admin troubleshooting
  • Custom IPAM agents that DLL-load into the Dhcp svchost
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("forescout","ciscoise","ipam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the spawned child's SHA256, command line, and the originating DHCP server IP from concurrent DeviceNetworkEvents (UDP/68 inbound). If the device is on a hostile/guest network or the DHCP server isn't the corporate one, escalate immediately. 2) Contain: isolate the device; switch to static IP on the perimeter VLAN until patched. Capture a memory dump of the dhcpcsvc svchost before reboot if possible — exploit chains often live only in-memory. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for any host receiving DHCP from an unexpected server in the same time bucket; check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for other unpatched CVE-2026-44815 hosts per UC1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-s Dhcp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "DhcpServer"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| extend ParentCmd = tostring(EventData)
| where ParentCmd has "-s Dhcp" and ParentCmd !has "DhcpServer"
| extend NewProc = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where NewProc !in ("conhost.exe","werfault.exe","werfaultsecure.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
title: Anomalous Child of DHCP Client svchost (CVE-2026-44815 Exploitation Indicator)
id: 8c3b9a52-7d4e-4f81-b2a6-1e9c0d4f5b73
description: svchost.exe hosting the Dhcp service spawning any child other than conhost/WerFault is a high-fidelity indicator of CVE-2026-44815 (Windows DHCP Client stack-based buffer overflow) being exploited via a crafted DHCP server reply.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-patches-record-206-flaws.html
  - https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-44815
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\svchost.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '-s Dhcp'
  filter_dhcp_server:
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'DhcpServer'
  filter_benign_children:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\conhost.exe'
      - '\WerFault.exe'
      - '\WerFaultSecure.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and not filter_dhcp_server and not filter_benign_children
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\svchost.exe OR *\SVCHOST.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*"-s Dhcp"* OR *"-s DHCP"*) -@ParentCommandLine:*DhcpServer* -@Image:(*\conhost.exe OR *\WerFault.exe OR *\WerFaultSecure.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/svchost\.exe$/i regex("-s Dhcp(\\b|$)", field=ParentCommandLine)
| NOT regex("DhcpServer", field=ParentCommandLine)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\(conhost|WerFault|WerFaultSecure)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="svchost.exe" AND Processes.parent_process="*-s Dhcp*" AND Processes.process_name!="conhost.exe" AND Processes.process_name!="WerFault.exe" AND Processes.process_name!="WerFaultSecure.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_integrity_level | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

GreenPlasma (CVE-2026-45586) — ctfmon.exe spawning child process AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for ctfmon.exe (Collaborative Translation Framework) acting as a parent process — Chaotic Eclipse's GreenPlasma PoC abuses CTF IPC for privilege escalation. ctfmon.exe legitimately never spawns child processes in user environments, so any child is a high-fidelity signal of CTF abuse. Rationale: Article identifies CVE-2026-45586 as the fix for Chaotic Eclipse's GreenPlasma exploit against the Collaborative Translation Framework (CTFMON). ctfmon.exe spawning anything is anomalous — the process exists to handle IME/language-bar IPC, not to launch executables; integrity-level elevation in the child is the kill-shot.
ATT&CKT1068 T1559
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IME vendor updaters (e.g. Microsoft Pinyin, Google Japanese IME) briefly invoked from ctfmon during install
  • Accessibility tooling that piggybacks on TSF/CTF IPC
  • Legacy applications using ITfThreadMgr COM with custom shells (very rare)
  • Lab/red-team machines running James Forshaw / Chaotic Eclipse PoCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32\\IME\\" and FileName !endswith "Update.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the integrity level of the child — Medium→High or User→SYSTEM jump confirms CTF abuse; pull DeviceImageLoadEvents for any unusual DLLs loaded into ctfmon.exe shortly before. 2) Contain: kill the spawned child, isolate the device, and verify the host has KB for CVE-2026-45586 installed; reset the logged-on user's credentials if any privileged child ran. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for ctfmon.exe parent across 30d; cross-reference with DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities to find hosts still missing the patch.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ctfmon.exe"
| where FileName !=~ "conhost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName =~ "ctfmon.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\ctfmon.exe"
| where TargetProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessIntegrityLevel, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
title: GreenPlasma PoC - ctfmon.exe Spawning Child Process (CVE-2026-45586)
id: 2a7b4c89-5d3e-4a91-8f6c-b2d4e8a91f53
description: Detects ctfmon.exe (Collaborative Translation Framework Loader) as a parent of any non-conhost process. Behaviour aligned with Chaotic Eclipse's GreenPlasma CTFMON privilege-escalation PoC fixed by Microsoft as CVE-2026-45586.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\ctfmon.exe OR *\CTFMON.EXE OR *\Ctfmon.exe) -@Image:(*\conhost.exe OR *\CONHOST.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/ctfmon\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\conhost\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="ctfmon.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_integrity_level IN ("high","system") OR process_name!="conhost.exe"
HTTP/2 Bomb (CVE-2026-49160) — IIS hosts missing MaxHeadersCount mitigation registry AIWeaponization Medium
Posture hunt for Windows IIS hosts that run w3wp.exe but have not configured the new MaxHeadersCount registry value introduced by Microsoft as the mitigation for the HTTP/2 Bomb HTTP.sys DoS (CVE-2026-49160). Unmitigated hosts can exhaust 64 GB of RAM in ~45 seconds per the Calif/Tenable analysis cited in the article. Rationale: Article quotes Microsoft introducing 'MaxHeadersCount' as the explicit registry-based mitigation for CVE-2026-49160 / HTTP/2 Bomb; presence-check the mitigation against the list of hosts actually running IIS (w3wp.exe) so the alert pool is bounded to genuinely exposed servers, not the whole fleet.
ATT&CKT1499.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IIS hosts running internal apps with no public exposure (still vulnerable but lower priority)
  • Servers where the MaxHeadersCount was set via group policy preferences and the registry-write event is older than the lookback
  • Decommissioned IIS roles where w3wp.exe ran historically but is now disabled
  • Containerised IIS where registry isolation hides the setting
  • Hosts under maintenance windows scheduled to receive the patch + mitigation in next cycle
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm IIS is actually serving traffic on the listed host (`Get-IISSite`); check public exposure via DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing and external attack-surface tooling. 2) Contain: apply the registry mitigation via GPO — set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters\MaxHeadersCount to 100 (or vendor-recommended value) and restart HTTP.sys; for internet-facing hosts, also enable WAF HTTP/2 header limits at the edge as defence in depth. 3) Hunt: search for prior IIS w3wp.exe memory-exhaustion crashes (Application event 1000 with w3wp faulting module HTTP.sys) and W3CIISLog spikes in csBytes that may indicate prior exploitation attempts.
let IIS_Hosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "w3wp.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
    | summarize by DeviceId, DeviceName;
let Mitigated = DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where RegistryKey has @"\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
    | where RegistryValueName =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
    | where toint(RegistryValueData) between (1 .. 1000)
    | summarize by DeviceId;
IIS_Hosts
| join kind=leftanti Mitigated on DeviceId
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSVersion) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSVersion, MitigationStatus = "MaxHeadersCount NOT set — vulnerable to HTTP/2 Bomb"
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
let IIS_Hosts = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
    | summarize by Computer;
let Mitigated = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventLog == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" and EventID == 13
    | where ParameterXml has @"\Services\HTTP\Parameters\MaxHeadersCount"
    | summarize by Computer;
IIS_Hosts
| join kind=leftanti Mitigated on Computer
| project Computer, MitigationStatus = "MaxHeadersCount NOT set — vulnerable to HTTP/2 Bomb (CVE-2026-49160)"
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\w3wp.exe OR *\W3WP.EXE) -@host:[host-list-with-MaxHeadersCount-set]
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/w3wp\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
| join({#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate regex("\\\\Services\\\\HTTP\\\\Parameters", field=RegObjectName) RegValueName=/MaxHeadersCount/i | groupBy([aid], function=count(as=Mitigated))}, field=aid, include=[Mitigated])
| Mitigated!=*
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Processes.dest) as IIS_Hosts from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="w3wp.exe" by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=left dest [| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\HTTP\\Parameters*" AND Registry.registry_value_name="MaxHeadersCount" by Registry.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | rename count as Mitigation_Set] | where isnull(Mitigation_Set)
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Processes.dest) as IIS_Hosts from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="w3wp.exe" by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=left dest [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\HTTP\\Parameters*" AND Registry.registry_value_name="MaxHeadersCount" by Registry.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | rename count as Mitigation_Set] | where isnull(Mitigation_Set)

| order by conn_count desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application

author: Clankerusecase

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Suspected phpBB OAuth Authentication Bypass Exploit Attempt (CVE-2026-29199) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests targeting phpBB OAuth login endpoints implicated in the CVE-2026-29199 single-request authentication bypass. Anchors on the patched OAuth handler path /user/oauth/authenticate/ disclosed in the release notes and phpBB's pre-existing /ucp.php login=external OAuth callback pattern, where high request volume from a single source indicates session-acquisition spraying against the public memberlist. Rationale: Anchored on the exact patched URI '/user/oauth/authenticate/' from the article's release-notes breaking-change callout and the pre-patch phpBB OAuth callback pattern (/ucp.php login=external oauth_service=). The article notes the attack is one HTTP request per user-id and the memberlist is public, so spraying produces high hit-count from one source — that's the cardinality threshold. Defender Advanced Hunting has no inbound HTTP web-access table; Datadog/Falcon equivalents would need a custom apache/nginx integration not in the schema reference, so left empty rather than guess at field paths.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users completing Google/Facebook/Microsoft OAuth sign-ins on a healthy phpBB forum with many users
  • Search-engine crawlers (Googlebot/Bingbot) hitting /ucp.php login pages
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors hammering forum login endpoints
  • Single-sign-on integration testing during phpBB extension development
  • Legacy unpatched mobile clients still pointing at old OAuth callback URL
Suppression filter
// Suppress known SSO providers and monitoring agents
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake")
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-soc-scanner-ip>","<known-monitoring-ip>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the phpBB instance version banner from /docs/CHANGELOG.html or response headers — if ≤3.3.16 or 4.0.0-a2, the host is vulnerable and any hits are presumed malicious. Correlate src IP against threat-intel and check whether new admin / moderator accounts appeared in the phpBB users table around the same window. Step 2 (contain): If unpatched, take the forum offline OR put a WAF rule in front blocking the OAuth callback paths until upgrade to 3.3.17 / master is applied. Force-invalidate all sessions in phpbb_sessions table and rotate the COOKIE secret. Step 3 (hunt): Query for new file writes under /cache, /store, /files, /ext on the web root (pivots to UC2) and for any web-server process spawning shells (UC3) in the 24h after the first suspicious request. Check for outbound exfil from the web host to unfamiliar destinations.
let WindowDays = 7d;
let phpBBHits =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(WindowDays)
    | where Url has_any ("/ucp.php", "/user/oauth/authenticate")
    | where Url has_any ("oauth_service=", "login=external", "mode=login") or Url contains "/user/oauth/authenticate/"
    | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","302","303");
phpBBHits
| summarize Hits = count(),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(Url),
            UrlSample = make_set(Url, 20),
            UAs = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where Hits > 10 or DistinctUrls > 5
| order by Hits desc

PHP Web Shell Drop in phpBB Writable Directory (Post-CVE-2026-29199 RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of PHP-executable files inside phpBB's standard writable subtrees (/cache, /store, /files, /images/avatars/upload, /ext) by PHP-interpreter or web-server processes. Once CVE-2026-29199 yields an administrator session, the article states RCE follows — web shells dropped into these phpBB-writable paths are the standard persistence mechanism. Rationale: Anchored on phpBB's documented writable directories (/cache, /store, /files, /images/avatars/upload, /ext) — these are the only paths where the web-server user typically has write permission, so a php-fpm or apache process creating a .php there outside of an upgrade window is unambiguous. Combined with the article's RCE outcome, this catches the install phase after CVE-2026-29199 admin takeover.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • phpBB 3.3.x → 3.3.17 upgrade script writing new PHP files into /install or /vendor during the patch rollout itself
  • Administrator installing a legitimate phpBB extension that drops PHP into /ext/<vendor>/<extname>
  • Composer/Packagist dependency install writing autoload files into /vendor
  • Style/theme installation dropping .php template files into /styles/<theme>/template/
  • phpBB cache regeneration on a high-traffic forum writing .php sql/lang files into /cache (these should be from cron, not from a web request)
Suppression filter
// Suppress maintenance-window upgrades and trusted extension installs
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("composer","install.php","/install/","phpbb_cli")
| where FolderPath !has "/vendor/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the newly-created file's contents — grep for `eval(`, `assert(`, `base64_decode(`, `gzinflate(`, `system(`, `passthru(`, `shell_exec(`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_POST['cmd']`, `preg_replace('/.+/e'`. Check the file's mtime against phpBB upgrade-window changetracker entries. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file (chmod 000 + move out of web-root), revoke and rotate phpBB admin passwords + config.php DB credentials, kill all sessions in phpbb_sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the web-server user account — list every file written by it in the last 30 days, list every outbound network connection from php-fpm/apache (UC3), and grep webserver access logs for the same source IPs/User-Agents that hit the OAuth endpoints (UC1).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7" or FileName endswith ".pht"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/phpbb/", @"\phpbb\", "/cache/", "/store/", "/files/", "/images/avatars/upload/", "/ext/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","phar","php5","php7","pht")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/phpbb/", @"\phpbb\", "/cache/", "/store/", "/files/", "/images/avatars/upload/", "/ext/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp","php-cgi","php.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web Server Process Spawning Shell or Network Tool (phpBB Post-RCE Execution) AIExploitation High
Detects shell interpreters or network download tools spawned as children of PHP / Apache / Nginx / IIS worker processes — the canonical execution signal after a web RCE. The article confirms CVE-2026-29199 chains to RCE on the latest 4.x; on a phpBB host this child-process pattern is the loudest evidence of successful exploitation. Rationale: Article explicitly states the chain ends in RCE on the latest 4.x. On any phpBB host (which is invariably a PHP-on-Apache/Nginx/IIS web tier), php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp spawning bash, curl, python, or nc is non-baseline almost everywhere — the parent set is exactly the processes phpBB runs under. Article-specific anchor: this is the FIRST process-tree shape an analyst should pivot on for any host running phpBB ≤3.3.16 / 4.0.0-a2 that took external HTTP after June 10, 2026.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • phpBB 3.3.x → 3.3.17 in-place upgrade triggering composer or php cli sub-processes during the patch window
  • Monitoring agents (Nagios/Datadog/Zabbix) running php-fpm health probes that wrap curl for self-checks
  • Extension install/uninstall via the phpBB admin panel that legitimately shells out to download dependencies
  • Backup cron jobs running under the web-server user that pipe through curl/wget to upload archives
  • phpBB cron-driven email notification flushers that spawn /bin/sh for sendmail
Suppression filter
// Suppress known maintenance + monitoring patterns
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("composer","phpbb_cli","healthcheck","--version")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cron"
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://packagist.org","https://repo.packagist.org","https://download.phpbb.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full child command-line and the parent's request URL if you have a CGI-correlated log (X-Request-ID / nginx combined log). Hash the child binary and check whether it was copied/dropped into /tmp or under the phpBB web-root (likely a staged dropper). Step 2 (contain): Kill the child PID, isolate the host from the internet (block the web server's egress except to package mirrors), force-rotate the phpbb config.php DB password and the OS web-user's authorized_keys. Capture memory before reboot. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the child's PID and trace any subsequent DnsRequest / NetworkConnectIP4 from it — that's where C2 lives. Cross-reference UC2 (web shell drop) on the same host within ±24h, and UC1 (OAuth bypass attempts) at the perimeter for the same source IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","busybox")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi","php.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PHP webshell file (<?php system) written to webroot by web-server process · [LLM] Web-server process modifying PHP / Apache / Nginx config or log files · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48030: Pheditor: OS Command Injection in terminal han

HTTP POST to pheditor.php terminal handler with shell metacharacters AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP POST traffic to the vulnerable /pheditor.php endpoint that carries the action=terminal selector and/or shell metacharacters (`;` `|` `` ` `` `$(` `&&` `||` `<` `>`). CVE-2026-48030 requires the attacker hit this exact endpoint with metacharacters in the dir parameter, so this is the cleanest pre-execution signal. Rationale: Article PoC step 4 sends `dir=/tmp; curl -s https://ifconfig.me #` via --data-urlencode against /pheditor.php with action=terminal. URI stem + method + presence of `action=terminal` and shell metacharacters in the request (URI or body where WAF captures it) is the highest-fidelity pre-execution signal because pheditor is a niche package; any POST to that URL is rare and the metachars do not appear in benign terminal use through the whitelist.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team / pentest exercises explicitly targeting the pheditor advisory
  • Legitimate developer using the pheditor terminal feature from a known admin IP (shell metacharacters like `;` can appear in benign commands too)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei) probing the GHSA template
  • Backup/automation scripts that POST to /pheditor.php with multi-command sequences
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<admin-bastion-ip>", "<scanner-ip>") and UserAgents !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "ZAP")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full WAF/IIS record for the POST — confirm action=terminal is present and what the dir/command values were. Check the source IP against tenant admin allow-list and recent auth logs (was a session legitimately established?). Step 2 (contain): If source IP is not an authorised admin, block at the WAF/perimeter, rotate the pheditor admin password, and remove `terminal` permission for affected users in pheditor config. Snapshot /var/www/ before any cleanup. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the web-server host — search DeviceProcessEvents/ImProcessCreate for php-fpm/apache2/nginx parents spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, nc within ±5 min of the POST; search DeviceFileEvents for new .php files written under the webroot; search outbound network from www-data to public IPs. Upgrade pheditor to a patched version or apply the `escapeshellarg($dir)` fix.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WebPosts = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where csUriStem endswith "/pheditor.php"
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | extend HasTerminalAction = tolong(csUriQuery has "action=terminal")
    | extend HasMetachar = tolong(csUriQuery matches regex @"[;|`<>]|%3B|%7C|%60|\$\(|%24%28|&&|%26%26|%7C%7C")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceIP=cIP, UserAgent=csUserAgent, Method=csMethod, Url=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, HasTerminalAction, HasMetachar;
let WafPosts = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where RequestURL has "/pheditor.php"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | extend HasTerminalAction = tolong(RequestURL has "action=terminal" or Message has "action=terminal")
    | extend HasMetachar = tolong(RequestURL matches regex @"[;|`<>]|\$\(|&&|\|\|" or Message matches regex @"[;|`<>]|\$\(|&&|\|\|")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP=SourceIP, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, Method=RequestMethod, Url=RequestURL, Query=RequestContext, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), HasTerminalAction, HasMetachar;
union isfuzzy=true WebPosts, WafPosts
| summarize POSTCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), HasTerminal=max(HasTerminalAction), HasMeta=max(HasMetachar), Targets=make_set(Computer, 5), UserAgents=make_set(UserAgent, 5), QueriesSample=make_set(Query, 5)
    by SourceIP
| where POSTCount >= 2 or HasTerminal == 1 or HasMeta == 1
| order by LastSeen desc

PHP-FPM / Apache / Nginx web-server parent spawning shell or download utility AIExploitation High
Detects PHP-FPM, Apache, Nginx, or php-cgi processes spawning sh/bash/curl/wget/nc/python — the post-injection execution shape from CVE-2026-48030 where shell_exec runs `cd $dir && $command && echo \ ; pwd` with attacker-controlled metacharacters. Legit PHP apps almost never shell out to download utilities. Rationale: Article PoC steps 4–5 invoke `cd /tmp; curl -s https://ifconfig.me #` and `cd /var/www/html; echo '<?php system(...)?>' > /var/www/html/shell.php #` — both fork sh from php-fpm. The Step 5 result `uid=33(www-data)` confirms execution context. Parent (php-fpm/apache/nginx) + child (sh/curl/wget) + injection-shaped command line is the unique fingerprint; legitimate PHP apps rarely shell out to download utilities.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer / npm post-install scripts running curl from the web server user during deploys
  • Health-check / monitoring scripts that exec curl from cron under www-data
  • Legitimate PHP apps using exec() / shell_exec() for image processing (ImageMagick, ffmpeg) — usually not curl/wget but worth allow-listing per-app
  • Backup scripts in /var/www/ that shell out to rsync/curl
  • WordPress plugin update routines that fetch over HTTP from a PHP context
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("composer","healthcheck","/usr/local/bin/wp ","ImageMagick","ffmpeg") and DeviceName !in ("<deploy-host>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the parent php-fpm PID and correlate with the web access log entry within ±5s — find the source IP and URL that triggered. Inspect the child's full command line for fetched URL / written path. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the web host from the network, suspend the www-data process, and snapshot /var/www/ and /tmp/ for forensics. Block the attacker IP and any external destination at the perimeter. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten under the webroot for new .php files created by web-server processes, and ImNetworkSession/NetworkConnectIP4 for outbound traffic from www-data to public IPs. Verify pheditor version and patch to a release ≥ 2.0.4 or apply escapeshellarg($dir).

PHP webshell file (<?php system) written to webroot by web-server process AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a .php / .phtml file under common Linux webroots (/var/www, /srv/www, /usr/share/nginx) by php-fpm, apache2, httpd, or nginx — the exact pattern from PoC step 5 where the attacker drops shell.php containing `<?php system($_GET["c"]);?>`. Rationale: PoC step 5 explicitly drops `<?php system($_GET["c"]);?>` to /var/www/html/shell.php via shell redirection from a php-fpm-spawned sh. File created under webroot + .php extension + creator process is a web-server binary is a near-zero-baseline event outside CMS auto-update flows, which are easy to allow-list.
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress / Drupal / Joomla automatic plugin or core updates (php-fpm writes new plugin .php files into wp-content/plugins/)
  • Composer-managed deploys that run as the web-server user and lay down vendor/*.php
  • CI/CD pipelines that sync built PHP artifacts under /var/www via the web-server account
  • Legitimate CMS file-managers (e.g. pheditor itself in approved admin use) writing .php under the webroot
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("wp-cron","composer install","composer update","drush ","artisan ") and TargetFilePath !has_any ("/wp-content/upgrade/","/wp-content/plugins/","/sites/default/files/php/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the created file and look for classic webshell primitives (`<?php` + system/exec/passthru/eval/$_GET/$_POST/$_REQUEST/base64_decode). Cross-reference creator process PID with web access logs for the originating HTTP request. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file (move outside the webroot, do not delete — preserve mtime/atime for IR), block the originating source IP, and rotate any credentials the web-server account had access to. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host — search for child processes spawned by the new webshell over the last 7d, outbound C2 from www-data, and other .php drops under the same path. Audit all pheditor installs across the fleet, disable terminal permission, and patch.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackHours)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcs)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/opt/lampp/htdocs/")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Pheditor RCE — PHP/web-server process outbound to public IP on non-web port AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound network connections from the web-server account (www-data, apache, nginx) to non-RFC1918 destinations on non-standard web ports (anything other than 80/443/8080/8443) — post-exploitation C2 / reverse shell / data-exfil behaviour expected after CVE-2026-48030 RCE. Rationale: Article impact section explicitly states the attacker gains code execution as the web-server user (`uid=33(www-data)` per PoC step 5). C2 / reverse-shell / payload-pull is the next attacker step, and a web-server account talking to a public IP on a non-web port is rare in production — most legit traffic from www-data is to 80/443 (APIs) or DNS/53. The detection avoids the false ImNetworkSession process-column predicates by pivoting on SrcUsername (web account) plus destination filtering.
ATT&CKT1095 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Database connections from web tier to RDS / MySQL / Postgres on 3306/5432 over public VPC endpoints (allow-list the DB IP)
  • SMTP/IMAP submission from CMS mail features (ports 25/465/587/993)
  • Outbound webhooks from CMS plugins to public APIs on non-standard ports (Twilio, Stripe, push providers)
  • NTP from misconfigured web hosts hitting public time servers on 123/udp
  • Container egress through public-facing NAT where the resolved IP is technically public
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr !in ("<rds-public-ip>","<smtp-relay-ip>") and DstPortNumber !in (3306, 5432, 25, 465, 587, 993, 123)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the public IP — check WHOIS, ASN, threat-intel feeds (VirusTotal, abuse.ch, GreyNoise). Pull the initiating process command line and recent web access logs for the host. Step 2 (contain): Block the destination IP/port at the perimeter, isolate the web host, terminate the process, and snapshot memory/disk if forensics warranted. Step 3 (hunt): Pull DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm-spawned shell children on the same host within ±10 min, check DeviceFileEvents for new .php under webroot, and pivot the destination IP across the fleet to find other compromised hosts. Patch pheditor and audit terminal permission across all installs.
let LookbackHours = 6h;
let WebProcs = dynamic(["php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","apache2","httpd","nginx","php-cgi","php","sh","bash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python3","python","perl","socat"]);
let WebUsers = dynamic(["www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","_www","www"]);
let AllowedPorts = dynamic([80,443,8080,8443,53]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackHours)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebProcs) or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ (WebUsers)
| where RemotePort !in (AllowedPorts)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackHours = 6h;
let WebUsers = dynamic(["www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","_www","www","php-fpm"]);
let AllowedPorts = dynamic([80,443,8080,8443,53]);

| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
| where SrcUsername has_any (WebUsers)
| where DstPortNumber !in (AllowedPorts)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server process modifying PHP / Apache / Nginx config or log files AIInstallation Medium
Detects php-fpm, apache2, httpd, nginx, or shell descendants writing to PHP/web-server configuration files (php.ini, .htaccess, .user.ini, apache2.conf, nginx.conf) or tampering with logs (chmod 000 /var/log/*, redirect to /dev/null) — the defense-evasion step an attacker takes after CVE-2026-48030 RCE to disable the TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist or hide their tracks. Rationale: Article notes the TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist is 'completely bypassed' — an attacker with www-data RCE will plausibly persist by editing php.ini (disable_functions, open_basedir), drop .htaccess for routing, or tamper with /var/log/apache2 access logs to hide the exploit POST. None of these files should be written by web-server processes during normal request handling. Sigma omitted because the detection is a union of file_event + process_creation (multi-shape).
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Salt) running as www-data on poorly-configured hosts
  • CMS plugins that legitimately write to .htaccess for URL-rewrite rules (WordPress permalinks, W3 Total Cache)
  • Log-rotation routines (logrotate) that as a side-effect touch /var/log/apache2 — though logrotate runs as root, not www-data
  • Developer ssh sessions performing config tweaks while shelled into a web host as www-data
  • Deploy pipelines copying nginx.conf into /etc/nginx/ during a release
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible-","puppet ","chef-client","salt-call","logrotate") and not (ActingProcessName == "sh" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "wp-cli")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the modified config file against the last known-good (etckeeper, git, backup) and inspect for added include directives, disable_functions tweaks, or auto_prepend_file pointers. For log tampering, check whether log entries before the modification time are missing or zero-bytes. Step 2 (contain): Restore the config from backup, kill the web-server user's shell, and rotate any credentials present in the config (DB passwords, API keys). Step 3 (hunt): Within ±15 min of the modification, pull all process activity by www-data, look for new persistence (cron, systemd units, .bash_profile/.bashrc under web-server home), and confirm no other webshells exist. Patch pheditor and review whether the web-server user actually needs write access to config paths (chown root + chmod 644 typically suffices).

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] IAM policy grant of cloudtrail/logs admin to unprivileged principal
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail StopLogging API call suspending audit trail delivery · [LLM] AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting CloudTrail log destination · [LLM] GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink (disabled=true) · [LLM] GCP log bucket deletion (DELETE_REQUESTED) via logging.buckets.delete · [LLM] AWS CloudTrail UpdateTrail with KMS key change (encryption-based log impairment)
AWS CloudTrail StopLogging API call suspending audit trail delivery AIActions on Objectives High
Detects invocation of the cloudtrail:StopLogging API, which halts log delivery from a trail to its S3 destination without deleting the trail itself. Per the Unit 42 article, this is the most direct evasion technique — an attacker with cloudtrail:StopLogging silently blinds downstream SIEM/SOAR/CSPM pipelines. Rationale: Article explicitly names the cloudtrail:StopLogging permission and stop-logging API as the Technique 1 evasion primitive. CloudTrail event name 'StopLogging' is the authoritative signal; success is the gating condition.
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR tabletop exercises where SOC pauses a trail intentionally
  • Account/region decommissioning workflow that stops trails before deletion
  • Automated remediation scripts that restart misconfigured trails (stop+start pattern)
  • Migration to AWS Organizations central trail (legacy account trail stopped)
Suppression filter
| where not (userIdentity.arn like /:role\/IncidentResponse-/ or userIdentity.arn like /:role\/break-glass/ or userIdentity.invokedBy = "AWS Internal")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the calling identity (userIdentity.arn + sessionContext.sessionIssuer), source IP, and userAgent. Cross-check against a known break-glass/IR allowlist and verify MFA was used. Compare against the last 90d of CloudTrail config changes for that trail. Step 2 — Contain: Immediately call StartLogging on the affected trail. If the caller is an IAM user or assumed-role session not on the allowlist, revoke the active session (DeactivateMFADevice + AttachUserPolicy AWSDenyAll, or revoke role sessions via revoke-sessions). Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the identity's CloudTrail activity in the 24h surrounding the StopLogging — look for DeleteBucket, UpdateTrail with kmsKeyId change, AttachUserPolicy granting cloudtrail:*, and any S3 GetObject/PutObject against the trail's log bucket. Check GuardDuty for related findings on the same principal.

| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType == "StopLogging"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

AWS S3 bucket deletion targeting CloudTrail log destination AIActions on Objectives High
Detects s3:DeleteBucket calls against buckets whose names match CloudTrail logging conventions (cloudtrail/audit/log substrings). Per the article, an attacker with s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject can delete the trail's S3 destination, which CloudTrail surfaces as a delivery-failure notification minutes later. Rationale: Article documents Technique 2: attacker with s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject deletes the trail's destination bucket. Name-pattern filter scopes to high-fidelity hits (most orgs' CloudTrail buckets follow the aws-cloudtrail-logs-* or *-audit-* convention).
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1070.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cleanup of orphaned trails after account-vending platform retires a sandbox
  • Terraform/CloudFormation destroy of an environment that included a CloudTrail bucket
  • Migration to centralized Organizations trail (legacy per-account buckets emptied + deleted)
  • Compliance-driven re-bucketing where the old bucket name contained 'audit'
Suppression filter
| where not (userIdentity.arn like /:assumed-role\/(TerraformDeploy|CloudFormationStackSet|AWSOrganizationsRoleClose)/ or userIdentity.invokedBy = "AWS Internal")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify whether the deleted bucket was an active CloudTrail destination by checking the trail config history (CloudTrail GetTrail/DescribeTrails for any trail referencing the bucket name). Pull the deleting principal's recent activity and MFA status. Step 2 — Contain: If the bucket was an active log destination, restore from cross-account log archive / Organizations central trail if available. Disable the deleting principal's keys (UpdateAccessKey Inactive) and revoke active sessions. Lock the destination bucket via S3 Object Lock + bucket policy denying DeleteBucket for any principal except a designated logging-admin role. Step 3 — Hunt: Look for PutBucketPolicy / DeleteBucketPolicy / PutBucketVersioning that preceded the delete (versioning often disabled first to allow object expunge). Pivot on the principal for StopLogging, UpdateTrail, DeleteTrail in the 24h surrounding.

| where ActionType == "DeleteBucket"
| where ObjectName has_any ("cloudtrail","audit","-log","aws-logs")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, ActivityObjects, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via UpdateSink (disabled=true) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink calls that flip the sink's disabled field to true, suspending log routing. Per the article, this is Google Cloud's equivalent of cloudtrail:StopLogging — a single config flip blinds the downstream pipeline. Rationale: Article explicitly cites the logging.sinks.update permission and the sink.disabled=true setting as Technique 1's GCP variant, with a confirming console message (Figure 1). Detection keys on the method name plus the boolean flip in the request payload.
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project owner pausing a noisy debug sink during cost-reduction effort
  • Migration of org-aggregated sink to a new destination (old one disabled then deleted)
  • Test environment where sinks are toggled programmatically
  • DLP/compliance team temporarily disabling a sink during PII redaction work
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("serviceaccount-terraform","deploy-pipeline","break-glass"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the calling principal (protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail), source IP, and the sink being disabled (protoPayload.resourceName). Cross-check the sink's filter to determine what telemetry just went dark (IAM, data-access, admin-activity). Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable the sink via UpdateSink disabled=false. If the principal is non-admin or operating from an unfamiliar IP/UA, suspend the service account (disable + rotate keys) or revoke the user's session via Cloud Identity admin. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the principal's gcloud audit activity ±2h for SetIamPolicy granting logging.admin, DeleteBucket on a log bucket, or any data-access events that the now-disabled sink would have captured. Inspect cloudaudit.googleapis.com/activity directly even if the sink fed an external SIEM.

GCP log bucket deletion (DELETE_REQUESTED) via logging.buckets.delete AIActions on Objectives High
Detects google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket calls against Cloud Logging buckets. The article notes deletion is deferred 7 days (DELETE_REQUESTED state), which means there's a recovery window — but the API call itself is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article documents Technique 2's GCP variant: logging.buckets.delete permission triggers DeleteBucket, putting the bucket in DELETE_REQUESTED for 7 days. The method name is canonical and rare in production, making it a clean alerting signal even without status filtering.
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1070
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project teardown where _Default and _Required buckets are intentionally removed
  • Migration to org-level log buckets (per-project buckets retired)
  • Re-region of log storage (delete + recreate in different location)
  • Terraform destroy of a sandbox project
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("terraform-deploy","cleanup-bot")) and AccountDisplayName !endswith "@cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the calling principal and the deleted bucket's name (protoPayload.resourceName) — note that _Required cannot be deleted, so any DeleteBucket against _Default or a custom analytics bucket is suspicious. Check the project's sink configuration: if sinks routed to that bucket, downstream destinations may also be affected. Step 2 — Contain: Because deletion is deferred 7 days, immediately call UndeleteBucket on the affected bucket and lock the bucket with iam.gserviceaccount.com role bindings restricting logging.buckets.delete to a designated logging-admin SA. Disable the offending principal's credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: Look for preceding SetIamPolicy granting roles/logging.admin to the principal, UpdateSink calls redirecting matching logs, and any data-access events the bucket would have captured. Pull the bucket's residual log contents before the 7-day purge.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Google Cloud Platform"
| where ActivityType has "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket" or ActionType has "DeleteBucket"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ActivityType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ActivityType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS CloudTrail UpdateTrail with KMS key change (encryption-based log impairment) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects UpdateTrail calls that swap the trail's KmsKeyId to an attacker-controlled or restricted KMS key, making subsequent log files unreadable to defenders even though logging continues. This implements Technique 4 from the article ('Impair Logging via Attacker-Controlled Encryption Key'). Rationale: Article's Technique 4 describes impairing logging via attacker-controlled encryption keys. UpdateTrail is the only CloudTrail API that accepts kmsKeyId, so any UpdateTrail event carrying that param is the high-fidelity hook. Hunt-tier because legitimate key rotation/migration also surfaces here.
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1486
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled KMS CMK rotation moving CloudTrail to a new key
  • Compliance project migrating CloudTrail to a customer-managed key (first-time encryption)
  • Cross-account log archive setup requiring a multi-region key
  • DR drill switching CloudTrail to a backup KMS key
Suppression filter
| where not (userIdentity.arn like /:assumed-role\/(KeyRotation|ComplianceMigration|TerraformDeploy)/) and requestParameters.kmsKeyId not like /:key\/(known-good-key-id-1|known-good-key-id-2)/
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Capture the old vs new kmsKeyId, the trail name, and the calling principal. Inspect the new key's policy (kms:GetKeyPolicy) — does it grant the SOC's analytics roles kms:Decrypt? If not, that's the smoking gun. Step 2 — Contain: If the new key blocks defender decrypt, restore the previous kmsKeyId via UpdateTrail. Lock the trail with a resource-based policy or AWS Organizations SCP requiring kmsKeyId to be in a known-good list. Revoke the offending principal's credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: Look for PutKeyPolicy / ScheduleKeyDeletion on the new key from the same principal, CreateKey events in the 24h prior, and any unusual cross-account kms:Encrypt activity. Verify historical log files in S3 are still readable (Decrypt test) — if not, escalate to IR for log-recovery procedure.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType == "UpdateTrail"
| where RawEventData has "kmsKeyId"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ActionType == "UpdateTrail"

| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ObjectName, RawEventData

IAM policy grant of cloudtrail/logs admin to unprivileged principal AIInstallation Medium
Detects AttachUserPolicy / AttachRolePolicy / PutUserPolicy / PutRolePolicy / CreatePolicy operations whose payload grants cloudtrail:*, logs:*, or logging.admin equivalents — the prerequisite for the article's evasion techniques. Implements reviewer feedback #3. Rationale: All techniques in the article presuppose the attacker holds cloudtrail:* / logging.admin permissions. Catching the IAM grant upstream gives defenders a chance to intervene before StopLogging/DeleteBucket fire. Sigma omitted because the policyDocument pattern requires substring search across nested JSON not cleanly expressible as a single selection block.
ATT&CKT1098.003 T1548.005
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding a new SOC analyst into the CloudTrail-read role
  • Terraform/CloudFormation rollout of central logging policies during platform upgrade
  • Break-glass role re-permissioning during IR
  • AWS Control Tower / Organizations creating service-linked roles with logging permissions
  • DevOps automation deploying a new log-aggregator service account
Suppression filter
| where not (userIdentity.arn like /:assumed-role\/(AWSControlTowerExecution|stacksets-exec-|AWSReservedSSO_PlatformAdmin)/ or userIdentity.invokedBy in ("cloudformation.amazonaws.com","AWS Internal"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Capture which principal granted what to whom (caller arn, target user/role, policy contents). Cross-check the target principal against your approved logging-admin allowlist (typically <5 named identities). Confirm the granter is itself authorized to make IAM changes — if not, you have a chained priv-esc. Step 2 — Contain: Revert the grant via DetachUserPolicy / DetachRolePolicy / DeletePolicyVersion. If the target is unknown, suspend the target principal's keys/sessions. Apply an SCP denying iam:Attach*Policy unless the policy ARN is on a known-good list (or condition aws:RequestTag/PolicyApproved=true). Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the target principal's CloudTrail activity in the next 24h — alert on any StopLogging/DeleteBucket/UpdateTrail/DeleteTrail it performs. Look at the granter's history for PassRole, AssumeRole into IAM-admin roles, and any AccessKey creation events. Check Identity Center / SSO logs for the original authentication.

| where Application in ("Amazon Web Services","Google Cloud Platform")
| where ActionType in ("AttachUserPolicy","AttachRolePolicy","PutUserPolicy","PutRolePolicy","CreatePolicy","CreatePolicyVersion","SetIamPolicy")
| where RawEventData has_any ("cloudtrail:*","cloudtrail:StopLogging","cloudtrail:DeleteTrail","cloudtrail:UpdateTrail","logs:*","logs:DeleteLogGroup","logging.admin","logging.configWriter","logging.buckets.delete","logging.sinks.update","AWSCloudTrail_FullAccess")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
