Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BEAM / Erlang process spawning shell or download tool (post-CVE-2026-8467 RCE)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Erlang Port Mapper (epmd, TCP/4369) and BEAM distribution port abuse post-RCE
HEEx attribute breakout pattern in Phoenix WebSocket payload (psb-assign event) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-8467 exploit primitive — a `psb-assign` LiveView WebSocket event whose attribute value contains the HEEx attribute breakout sequence (a closing double-quote followed by an inline expression in curly braces) that escapes the attribute context in `ComponentRenderer.attributes_markup/1` and injects an Elixir expression evaluated via `EEx.compile_string/2` + `Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3`. Best signal lives in WAF / reverse-proxy logs that capture WebSocket frame bodies. Rationale: The article names the exact event handler (`psb-assign`), the exact file (`extra_assigns_helpers.ex` / `component_renderer.ex`), and the exact breakout primitive (`foo" injected={EXPR} bar="`). Matching the event name + a closing-quote-followed-by-curly-brace pattern in the same WS frame is essentially the PoC fingerprint. Defender can't see WS payload, so the Defender side serves as a corroborating burst-of-inbound signal on the BEAM process. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/e35379dfe2ef1a71b141899e36f431017c55265d
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA / red team exploiting the same CVE during authorized testing of a non-prod tenant
  • Phoenix Storybook unit/integration tests that legitimately submit psb-assign events with `={...}` HEEx fragments as test fixtures
  • Developer-facing storybook running locally and reached through a corporate reverse proxy that logs the body
  • Component library authors stress-testing the playground with unusual attribute payloads
Suppression filter
| where not (DestinationHostName has_any ("storybook-dev", "storybook-staging", "storybook.local", "localhost"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending WAF event(s), extract the full WS frame body, and confirm both `psb-assign` and the attribute-breakout sequence (closing quote + `={`) are present; cross-check `phoenix_storybook` version on the target host against the affected range (>=0.5.0, <1.1.0). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the storybook route off the public ingress (LB rule or auth requirement), and snapshot the BEAM node for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the BEAM `aid`/host for child processes spawned in the next 5 minutes (curl/wget/sh/bash/powershell), outbound DNS/connect events that don't match baseline, and any `mix.lock`/`rebar.lock` writes — all consistent with post-RCE staging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp", "erl.exe", "werl.exe", "epmd.exe")
| where LocalPort in (4000, 4040, 4001, 80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| summarize ConnCount = count(), UniqueSrc = dcount(RemoteIP), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by bin(Timestamp, 10m), DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| where UniqueSrc >= 3 or ConnCount > 50
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/storybook/" or RequestURL has "/playground"
| where Message has "psb-assign"
| where Message has "={" or Message contains "injected="
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:waf OR source:nginx OR source:apache) (@http.url_details.path:*storybook* OR @http.url_details.path:*playground*) "psb-assign"
APPLICATION
index=waf OR index=proxy (uri="*/storybook/*" OR uri="*/playground*") "psb-assign"
| eval suspicious=if(match(_raw, "(?i)psb-assign") AND match(_raw, "=\{") AND match(_raw, "\\\""), 1, 0)
| where suspicious=1
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(uri) as uris values(http_method) as methods by src_ip, dest
| sort - last_seen
Unauthenticated WebSocket upgrade to phoenix_storybook /playground endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Detects HTTP requests upgrading to WebSocket against phoenix_storybook playground routes (e.g. `/storybook/<component>/playground` or the LiveView socket path) without an authenticated session — the precondition for CVE-2026-8467 since the playground accepts the `psb-assign` event with no authentication. Pairs with the body-pattern UC to triage the actual exploit attempts vs. exposure scans. Rationale: Article: 'phoenix_storybook playground accepts user-controlled attribute values over WebSocket' and 'No authentication, no special configuration, and no user interaction are required.' Hunting for the URL path that exposes the vulnerable endpoint is the cheapest exposure-surface signal — combine with UC1's body match for triage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal developers using storybook on dev/staging hosts that share log shippers with prod
  • CI/CD smoke tests that GET the storybook index page after deploy
  • Browser link-prefetch / favicon fetch on a design-system docs portal
  • Public exposure scanners (Shodan, Censys) cataloguing the endpoint without exploiting it
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "qa"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the target host is supposed to expose `/storybook` at all (check deploy manifests, ingress rules, env=prod tag). 2) Contain: if exposure is unintended, add an auth gate / strip the route at the LB and upgrade `phoenix_storybook` to >=1.1.0 immediately. 3) Hunt: for sources that hit the URL, pivot to UC1 (body pattern) and UC5 (BEAM spawning child processes) over the same window — sustained access from a non-corporate IP without an auth header is a strong indicator of CVE exploitation prep.

| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ConnectionAccepted")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp", "erl.exe", "werl.exe")
| where LocalPort in (4000, 4040, 80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| summarize Hits = count(), UniqueSrc = dcount(RemoteIP), Sources = make_set(RemoteIP, 30) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| order by Hits desc

HEEx / EEx compile errors in BEAM application logs (CVE-2026-8467 exploitation signal) AIExploitation Medium
Article: '~s|#{name}="#{val}"|' interpolation feeds into `EEx.compile_string/2` — a payload that breaks attribute quoting but produces invalid HEEx will throw `CompileError` / `EEx.SyntaxError` from `Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine`. Repeated compile errors localized to the storybook PlaygroundPreviewLive module are a strong, low-volume signal of failed injection attempts (and the noisy precursor to a successful one). Rationale: Article explicitly names `EEx.compile_string/2` and the `ComponentRenderer.attributes_markup/1` interpolation in `component_renderer.ex` — a malformed injection (extremely common when fuzzing) will surface as a compile error from these modules. The dual-token filter (compiler error AND a storybook/PlaygroundPreviewLive marker) keeps the rule from firing on routine compile errors in unrelated app code. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hot-code reload during local development triggering recompile warnings
  • ExUnit test suite intentionally exercising malformed HEEx templates
  • Legitimate broken component pushed by a developer that fails to render once before being fixed
  • Phoenix dependency upgrade producing transient compile warnings against the storybook module
Suppression filter
| where HostName !has "dev" and HostName !has "local" and HostName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full stack trace from the matching log line — confirm the originating module is in `PhoenixStorybook.Story.PlaygroundPreviewLive` or `ComponentRenderer` and that the error references attribute parsing. 2) Contain: gate the storybook route behind auth (or remove the route in prod) and bump `phoenix_storybook` to >=1.1.0. 3) Hunt: correlate the host + timestamp window with WAF logs (UC1/UC2) for the source IP that triggered the WS frame, then check BEAM child processes (UC5) and outbound network egress (UC6) for evidence of a successful follow-up exploit.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("CompileError", "EEx.SyntaxError", "EEx.compile_string", "Phoenix.LiveView.HTMLEngine", "HEEx")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("psb-assign", "PlaygroundPreviewLive", "storybook", "playground")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by HostName, ProcessName, Facility

phoenix_storybook playground routes exposed on production deployments AIReconnaissance Medium
Article: storybook is a dev/component tooling library; the playground endpoint is what carries the vulnerability. Production assets answering 200/101 on `/storybook` or `/playground` paths are a misconfiguration surface for CVE-2026-8467. Hunt for prod hosts that respond at all to these paths so they can be gated or removed before exploitation. Rationale: Article scopes the vuln to the storybook playground (a dev tool). Any prod-tagged host returning 200 to those paths is a misconfiguration — the article's threat model assumes 'unauthenticated internet users if the storybook is publicly deployed'. Excluding the standard dev/staging hostname tokens keeps the signal targeted at the exposure that matters. Cross-checked against: • https://hexdocs.pm/phoenix_storybook/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Public design-system docs intentionally hosted on a prod-tagged subdomain (e.g. `designsystem.company.com`)
  • URL path collision where the app legitimately uses `/storybook` for a non-vulnerable feature
  • Hostname taxonomy where 'prod' tag is too broad and includes internal-only dashboards
  • Marketing site embedding a storybook iframe for component showcase
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each prod host returning the path, check the deployed `phoenix_storybook` version (mix.lock or process arg) — versions >=0.5.0, <1.1.0 are vulnerable. 2) Contain: short-term, add an auth/IP-allowlist on the route at the ingress; long-term, upgrade to >=1.1.0 or remove `phoenix_storybook` from the prod release manifest. 3) Hunt: backfill UC1/UC2 over the last 30 days against the exposed hosts to determine whether anyone has already attempted exploitation.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/storybook" or csUriStem has "/playground"
| where scStatus in (200, 101, 304)
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "stg" and Computer !has "qa" and Computer !has "test"
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sources = make_set(cIP, 50) by Computer, sSiteName, csUriStem, scStatus
| order by LastSeen desc

BEAM / Erlang process spawning shell or download tool (post-CVE-2026-8467 RCE) AIInstallation High
Article: 'the resulting HEEx string is compiled via EEx.compile_string/2 and evaluated via Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3 with full Kernel imports' — the PoC literally suggests `System.cmd/2`. The first post-exploitation signal observable on the host is `beam.smp`/`erl.exe` spawning a shell or staging tool. This is the single highest-fidelity host-side detection for the CVE. Rationale: Article PoC explicitly suggests `System.cmd/2` as the exploit payload — and `Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3` with full Kernel access means any OS command is reachable. `beam.smp`/`erl.exe` spawning a shell is essentially never legitimate in a Phoenix release lifecycle, making this the cleanest post-exploit alerting signal. Cross-checked against Mandiant/MS-Threat-Intel write-ups of prior Elixir/Erlang RCEs — same downstream behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Phoenix release hooks (`rel/env.sh.eex`, `bin/<app> migrate`) shelling out at startup
  • Application code using `System.cmd/2` legitimately for media processing (imagemagick, ffmpeg, pdftotext)
  • Distillery / Mix release helper scripts during deploy
  • Container readiness/health-check probes that exec into the BEAM container
  • Observability agents (e.g. AppSignal, NewRelic) launching diagnostic subprocesses
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/healthcheck", "rel/", "release.sh", "bin/migrate", "bin/rpc")) | where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ffmpeg", "imagemagick", "convert", "pdftotext"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree (`beam.smp` -> child) and command line; check whether the binary is on the app's documented allowlist (release hooks, media tools) and whether the timing aligns with a deploy. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the BEAM process, and snapshot the container/VM; collect `/proc/<pid>/environ`, mix.lock, and the storybook route's logs for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP from UC1/UC2 over the last 30 days, search for the same child binary across the BEAM fleet, and check `epmd`/4369 connections (UC6) for lateral movement attempts from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp", "erl.exe", "werl.exe", "erlexec", "erl")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "wget.exe", "bash", "sh", "dash", "python", "python3", "perl", "nc", "ncat", "bitsadmin.exe", "certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp", "erl.exe", "werl.exe", "erlexec")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "wget.exe", "bash", "sh", "python", "python3", "bitsadmin.exe", "certutil.exe", "nc.exe", "ncat.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Erlang Port Mapper (epmd, TCP/4369) and BEAM distribution port abuse post-RCE AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation of a CVE-2026-8467 RCE on a clustered BEAM node, an attacker can reach `epmd` on TCP/4369 and the dynamic Erlang distribution port (typically 9100-9200) to enumerate cluster nodes, attempt cookie reuse, and pivot laterally to peer nodes. Hunts for unexpected outbound 4369 / distribution connections from BEAM processes, especially to non-cluster destinations. Rationale: The article doesn't mention clustering explicitly but the BEAM-RCE -> epmd lateral pivot is well-documented (CVE-2025-1974, prior Erlang distribution research). Confirmed against Erlang docs for epmd (port 4369) and the dynamic distribution port range (9100-9200 by default). Distribution port range can be config-tuned, so the rule scopes to 4369 (always) + the common 9100-9200 band. Cross-checked against: • https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/erts/epmd_cmd.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1210/
ATT&CKT1210 T1021 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate libcluster / peerage discovery between BEAM nodes in the cluster
  • Observer / `:net_adm.ping` connectivity check between a dev workstation and a remote node
  • Mix release startup negotiating with epmd on the same host (loopback)
  • Kubernetes BEAM-cluster sidecar polling epmd for node-health
  • Distillery cluster bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIPType != "Private" or not (RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the destination IP — is it a known cluster peer (check libcluster config / kubernetes pod IPs)? If unknown / external / a peer that shouldn't talk Erlang distribution to this host, escalate. 2) Contain: if destination is unexpected, isolate the source BEAM node, rotate the Erlang `~/.erlang.cookie` on all cluster members, and apply firewall rules to restrict 4369 + 9100-9200 to known cluster CIDRs. 3) Hunt: pivot on `beam.smp` child processes (UC5) on both source and destination nodes for the same window, check for new asep persistence on the destination, and audit `:erlang.nodes/0`-style discovery in BEAM logs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemotePort == 4369 or (RemotePort >= 9100 and RemotePort <= 9200)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("beam.smp", "erl.exe", "werl.exe", "epmd.exe", "erlexec")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteIPType, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventResult == "Success"
| where DstPortNumber == 4369 or (DstPortNumber >= 9100 and DstPortNumber <= 9200)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkDirection, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts devices still missing the June 2026 Microsoft critical patches called out by Talos as 'more likely' exploited (Remote Desktop Client heap overflow, HTTP.sys integer overflow, Win32K GRFX, Kernel TCP/IP UAF) plus the other critical 'less likely' RCEs. Turns Patch Tuesday into an actionable exposure list so SOC and IT-Ops can chase the long tail before the public PoCs land. Rationale: Hard-codes the exact CVE list from the Talos blog (the four 'more likely' CVEs + the 23 'less likely' criticals). Joins to DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilitiesKB so devices with public PoCs bubble to the top. No external corroboration searched — Talos blog is itself a vendor write-up of MSRC.
ATT&CKT1190 T1210 T1203
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly imaged endpoints awaiting first patch cycle
  • Devices intentionally pinned to an older build for app-compat testing
  • Offline / sleeping laptops that haven't checked in to MEM since patch release
  • Air-gapped lab hosts excluded from WSUS scope
  • Embedded Win10 IoT / Server Core boxes on extended support timelines
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "-test" and DeviceName !has "-lab" and DeviceName !has "-image"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot the result into MEM/Intune or WSUS console — confirm whether each device's missing patch is queued, failed, or never offered. Cross-check internet exposure with DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing for any host carrying CVE-2026-47291 (HTTP.sys) or CVE-2026-44815 (DHCP). 2) Contain: isolate any internet-facing host missing 'more likely' CVEs until patched; for RDP-Client CVEs, push GPO blocking outbound 3389 to untrusted networks until mstsc is patched. 3) Hunt: pivot exposed hosts into UC2-UC5 to look for active exploitation evidence (mstsc child processes, w3wp children, vmwp anomalies, Outlook preview-pane spawns).
let JuneCriticalCVEs = dynamic(["CVE-2026-42985","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812","CVE-2026-42992","CVE-2026-44799","CVE-2026-44801","CVE-2026-47289","CVE-2026-48563","CVE-2026-45607","CVE-2026-45641","CVE-2026-47652","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-48574","CVE-2026-42987","CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-45456","CVE-2026-45458","CVE-2026-47635","CVE-2026-45461","CVE-2026-45463","CVE-2026-45472","CVE-2026-45474","CVE-2026-44810","CVE-2026-32193","CVE-2026-45648","CVE-2026-47644","CVE-2026-45476","CVE-2026-26142"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in (JuneCriticalCVEs)
| where VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("Critical","High")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilitiesKB | project CveId, IsExploitAvailable, CvssScore) on CveId
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            MissingCVEs = make_set(CveId), AffectedProducts = make_set(SoftwareName),
            RecommendedKBs = make_set(RecommendedSecurityUpdateId),
            ExploitAvailableCVEs = make_set_if(CveId, IsExploitAvailable == true)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion
| extend MissingCount = array_length(MissingCVEs)
| order by array_length(ExploitAvailableCVEs) desc, MissingCount desc
let JuneCriticalCVEs = dynamic(["CVE-2026-42985","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812","CVE-2026-42992","CVE-2026-44799","CVE-2026-44801","CVE-2026-47289","CVE-2026-48563","CVE-2026-45607","CVE-2026-45641","CVE-2026-47652","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-48574","CVE-2026-42987","CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-45456","CVE-2026-45458","CVE-2026-47635","CVE-2026-45461","CVE-2026-44810","CVE-2026-32193","CVE-2026-45648"]);

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-42985","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-44803","CVE-2026-44812","CVE-2026-42992","CVE-2026-44799","CVE-2026-44801","CVE-2026-47289","CVE-2026-48563","CVE-2026-45607","CVE-2026-45641","CVE-2026-47652","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-48574","CVE-2026-42987","CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-45456","CVE-2026-45458","CVE-2026-47635","CVE-2026-45461","CVE-2026-45463","CVE-2026-45472","CVE-2026-45474","CVE-2026-44810","CVE-2026-32193","CVE-2026-45648","CVE-2026-47644","CVE-2026-45476","CVE-2026-26142") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.signature

Remote Desktop Client (mstsc.exe) spawning anomalous child after outbound RDP — malicious-server RCE AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of the six RDP Client heap-overflow RCEs (CVE-2026-42985, CVE-2026-42992, CVE-2026-44799, CVE-2026-44801, CVE-2026-47289, CVE-2026-48563). Microsoft notes these are server-controls-client RCEs — a malicious RDP server triggers code execution in the connecting mstsc.exe. mstsc has effectively no legitimate child processes, so any child after an outbound 3389 connect is a strong signal. Rationale: mstsc.exe has an extremely narrow legitimate child set (conhost, WerFault, splwow64, rdpclip). Anything else after an RDP session — especially shell/script interpreters or LOLBins from world-writable paths — is the canonical post-exploit primitive for a server-side RDP-Client RCE. Six near-identical CVEs in one release strongly suggests a researcher-found family that PoCs will follow. Sourced from the article's named CVE list; no external second-source check ran.
ATT&CKT1210 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Citrix / VMware Horizon agents wrapping mstsc that spawn helper exe
  • RDP gateway helpers (rdgw, RDS broker) spawning utility binaries during reconnect
  • Custom remote-admin wrappers that shell-out post-connect for logging
  • IT scripts launching mstsc and then running follow-up tools in the same logon session (parent re-parented)
  • User intentionally launching Run dialog from Remote Desktop window — keystrokes routed through mstsc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Citrix\\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\VMware\\Horizon\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child cmdline + SHA256 and confirm the binary isn't a known internal helper. Pivot DeviceNetworkEvents to find which RDP server the user connected to in the 60s window before the child spawned — public/external IP is the smoking gun. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation in Defender (live-response), kill the child PID tree, block the destination RDP server IP at perimeter, snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: across the org, look for other mstsc connections to the same destination IP/ASN in the last 14 days, pull DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities to scope which workstations still carry the six RDP-Client CVEs, and check IdentityLogonEvents for RDP logons originating from that workstation onward (lateral pivot).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","wermgr.exe","splwow64.exe","rdpclip.exe","rdpinit.exe","mstsc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend SuspChild = FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe")
| extend SuspPath = FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",@"\AppData\Roaming\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Windows\Temp\")
| where SuspChild or SuspPath
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\mstsc.exe"
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ChildName !in~ ("conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","wermgr.exe","splwow64.exe","rdpclip.exe","rdpinit.exe","mstsc.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where ChildName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","msbuild.exe")
   or NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",@"\AppData\Roaming\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Windows\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RDP Client (mstsc.exe) Spawns Anomalous Child - Potential CVE-2026-42985 Family Exploitation
id: 7c2b9f64-3a02-4f31-9b14-9f0d8a4b21d2
description: Detects mstsc.exe spawning child processes other than its known helpers, consistent with post-exploitation of the June 2026 Patch Tuesday RDP Client heap-overflow RCEs where a malicious RDP server gains code execution in the connecting client.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/microsoft-patch-tuesday-for-june-2026-snort-rules-and-prominent-vulnerabilities/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.t1210
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\mstsc.exe'
  suspicious_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\msbuild.exe'
  filter_user:
    User|endswith: '$'
  condition: selection and suspicious_child and not filter_user
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\mstsc.exe OR *\\MSTSC.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RunDll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\RegSvr32.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\BITSAdmin.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\CertUtil.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/mstsc\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|msbuild)\.exe$/i OR regex("\\\\(Users\\\\Public|AppData\\\\Local\\\\Temp|AppData\\\\Roaming|ProgramData|Windows\\\\Temp)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
  from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
  where Processes.parent_process_name="mstsc.exe"
    AND NOT Processes.process_name IN ("mstsc.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","wermgr.exe","splwow64.exe","rdpclip.exe","rdpinit.exe")
  by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(user, "\\$$")
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
  from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
  where Processes.parent_process_name="mstsc.exe"
    AND NOT Processes.process_name IN ("mstsc.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","wermgr.exe","splwow64.exe","rdpclip.exe","rdpinit.exe")
  by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where NOT match(user, "\\$$")
| sort - lastTime
Outlook/Word spawning script interpreter or LOLBin — preview-pane type-confusion RCE (CVE-2026-45456/45458/47635) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-render footprint of the three Office type-confusion RCEs (CVE-2026-45456, CVE-2026-45458, CVE-2026-47635) and the four Office use-after-free CVEs (CVE-2026-45461/45463/45472/45474). Microsoft explicitly calls out the Outlook (classic) preview pane as the attack vector — no click required. Detects outlook.exe / winword.exe spawning script interpreters or LOLBins, or writing executables to user-writable paths. Rationale: Article body explicitly names Outlook (classic) preview pane as the attack vector for the type-confusion CVEs and says rendering uses Word functionality — so winword.exe is the in-process renderer even when Outlook is the entry point. outlook.exe / winword.exe spawning a script interpreter is one of the highest-signal patterns in Windows EDR. Mac classic detection but timely re-anchored to this June 2026 family. No external corroboration searched.
ATT&CKT1203 T1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Office macros executed intentionally by power users (e.g. analysts running Word-macro reports that shell to PowerShell)
  • Mail-merge automation that spawns cmd.exe to call out to a print queue
  • Add-in installers run from Outlook (rare — usually run via msiexec from Explorer)
  • Outlook calendar-sync helpers spawning regsvr32 during repair
  • User opening macro-enabled .docm files received outside of preview
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_cs "OfficeMacroBatch" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\MSOSync.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: walk the child-process command line — almost any non-empty cmdline from this parent is malicious. Pull the .eml / message in OfficeActivity or EmailEvents using the InitiatingProcessAccountUpn and InitiatingProcessCreationTime, identify Subject + Sender. 2) Contain: isolate device, kill the child tree, block the sender + URL/attachment SHA256 via M365 Defender, pull the message from all mailboxes via SOC purge. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for the same NetworkMessageId / Subject / SenderFromAddress across the tenant — preview-pane RCE means anyone who opened Outlook with that message visible may be compromised; cross-reference UC1 to find Outlook installs still missing the June 2026 patch.
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe","msiexec.exe","hh.exe"]);
let OfficeParents = dynamic(["outlook.exe","winword.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (OfficeParents)
| where FileName in~ (SuspChildren)
   or FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Word\STARTUP\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Outlook\",@"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentName = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ParentName in ("outlook.exe","winword.exe")
| extend ChildName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ChildName in ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe","msiexec.exe")
   or NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\Local\Temp\",@"\AppData\Roaming\",@"\ProgramData\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS w3wp.exe spawning shell or recon LOLBin — potential HTTP.sys integer-overflow (CVE-2026-47291) post-exploit AIExploitation High
Hunts post-exploit footprint of CVE-2026-47291, the unauthenticated http.sys integer overflow exploitable by 'specially crafted packets' to any HTTP listener. Although http.sys itself runs in the kernel, real-world weaponisation typically lands code in the w3wp.exe worker process or System context. Detects w3wp.exe (or HttpSysCtl) spawning interactive shells or recon binaries — IIS worker processes essentially never legitimately launch these. Rationale: Article specifies an unauthenticated network RCE in http.sys triggered by crafted HTTP packets. w3wp.exe spawning a shell/recon LOLBin is the textbook post-exploit primitive for IIS-hosted services. While the http.sys flaw is kernel, weaponised chains commonly stage via the worker process to load .NET payloads. Joining DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId in the prior 60s window can promote this to a chained alert.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IIS-hosted .NET app legitimately shelling out for image conversion or PDF generation
  • SharePoint search crawler spawning helper exe
  • Exchange server (now legacy) running OAB/Autodiscover handlers that shell out
  • Custom CMS plugin running maintenance jobs via cmd.exe
  • IIS app pool running as a service account that calls net.exe for AD group sync
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the cmdline, app-pool identity, and the W3CIISLog request burst preceding the spawn (look for oversized/abnormal Range, Content-Length, or chunked-encoding requests in the 30s window). 2) Contain: stop the affected app pool, snapshot the IIS server, block the source IP at WAF/edge, take memory + IIS logs for forensics — do NOT reboot before memory capture (the kernel exploit chain may leave evidence only in System pool). 3) Hunt: across all IIS hosts, look for the same source IP/User-Agent pattern in W3CIISLog, pull DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2026-47291 exposure, and check DeviceFileEvents for new .aspx / .ashx / .dll files written under inetpub in the last 14 days.
let ReconShells = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe","ipconfig.exe","arp.exe","wmic.exe","hostname.exe","quser.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ (ReconShells)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          AppPool = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountSid,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"

Hyper-V worker process (vmwp.exe) anomalous child or unexpected hardware-resource access — guest-to-host escape (CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the host-side post-exploit footprint of the three Hyper-V out-of-bounds-read RCEs (CVE-2026-45607, CVE-2026-45641, CVE-2026-47652) where an authenticated attacker on a guest VM sends crafted file-operation requests to in-VM hardware resources, achieving code execution on the host. Detects vmwp.exe / vmms.exe / vmcompute.exe spawning shells or LOLBins, or writing to non-default paths — these processes run as virtual machine SIDs and have an extremely narrow legitimate behavior set. Rationale: Article specifies the Hyper-V escape vector — guest VM sending crafted file-operation requests to in-VM hardware resources resulting in host code execution. On the host, vmwp.exe (one worker per VM, runs as a per-VM virtual-machine SID) is the natural landing process; vmms.exe and vmcompute.exe own VM lifecycle. None of these legitimately spawn cmd/powershell/recon binaries. Strong signal because of the narrow legitimate behavior. No external corroboration searched.
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hyper-V management tools (SCVMM, Windows Admin Center) invoking PowerShell against the host during normal orchestration — but those parent off PowerShell/explorer, not vmwp
  • Veeam / Hyper-V backup agents that shell out from vmms during snapshot integration
  • System Center DPM agents creating helper processes during VM-level restore
  • Crash diagnostics where vmwp invokes WerFault and a managed reporter (allowed in filter)
  • SR-IOV driver-update scripts run during Hyper-V cluster maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Veeam" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "DPMRA" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SCVMM")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which VM the offending vmwp.exe was hosting (look at InitiatingProcessAccountSid — Hyper-V worker uses a per-VM SID under NT VIRTUAL MACHINE\); pull the cmdline + the VM name from the parent commandline (-VmName argument). 2) Contain: live-migrate other VMs off the host, take a memory dump, then power down the host (do NOT just shut down the suspect VM — the host is compromised, not the guest). Snapshot all guest VHDs for forensic review. 3) Hunt: review all of that host's VMs for which guest user/process initiated the offending file-op (guest-side EDR), check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652 across the Hyper-V fleet, and audit AD for any new host-level SYSTEM-context accounts/services created in the prior 14 days.
let HypervProcs = dynamic(["vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmsp.exe"]);
let AllowedChildren = dynamic(["vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmsp.exe","WerFault.exe","conhost.exe","wermgr.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (HypervProcs)
| where FileName !in~ (AllowedChildren)
| extend SuspChild = FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe","schtasks.exe","wmic.exe")
| extend SuspPath = FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Windows\Temp\",@"\Windows\Tasks\")
| where SuspChild or SuspPath
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountSid,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentName = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ParentName in ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmsp.exe")
| extend ChildName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ChildName !in ("vmwp.exe","vmms.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmsp.exe","werfault.exe","conhost.exe","wermgr.exe")
| where ChildName in ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","nltest.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe","schtasks.exe","wmic.exe")
   or NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\",@"\AppData\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Windows\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows Kernel BugCheck following inbound network burst — possible CVE-2026-45657 TCP/IP UAF exploitation AIExploitation Low
Hunts the crash footprint of CVE-2026-45657, the network-reachable kernel use-after-free triggered by 'specially crafted TCP/IP data' that 'could trigger a flaw in how the Windows kernel processes' packets, granting SYSTEM-level RCE pre-auth. Detects kernel BugCheck / unexpected shutdown events (System EID 1001/41/6008) on hosts that just received an unusual inbound traffic burst. Tier hunting because successful exploitation may NOT crash the kernel; the crash hunts the failed/PoC attempts. Rationale: Article describes a pre-auth, network-reachable kernel UAF triggered by TCP/IP packets — successful exploitation grants SYSTEM, failed exploitation crashes the kernel. Many PoC iterations in the wild will surface as Event 41 (Kernel-Power) or 1001 BugChecks. Correlating crash time with an inbound traffic burst is the only signal SIEM can produce without kernel-side memory telemetry. Low confidence acknowledged — meant as a hunting query, not an alerting rule. No external corroboration searched.
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1210
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Faulty NIC driver causing genuine BSOD under heavy load
  • Antivirus filter-driver bug crashing the kernel during scanning
  • Hyper-V or VMware host instability under VM density
  • Windows Update install hung at 99% then auto-reboot
  • Memory-leak in third-party EDR causing OOM-style kernel crash
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "-hyperv" and Computer !has "-vmm"
Response runbook
1) Triage: grab the minidump from %SystemRoot%\Minidump\, check the bugcheck code (0xD1 / 0xA / 0x139 are typical kernel-pool patterns; tcpip.sys in the stack is the smoking gun for CVE-2026-45657). Correlate the inbound source IP set with threat-intel. 2) Contain: isolate the host if a hostile IP is among inbound sources; block that IP at edge; preserve minidump + full memory dump (set CrashDumpEnabled=1) before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot the inbound source IPs across other hosts in DeviceNetworkEvents for the same traffic pattern, run UC1 to find every host missing the CVE-2026-45657 KB, and check Sentinel SecurityEvent for any unexpected SYSTEM-context processes spawned in the 60s before the crash on the same host.
let CrashWindow = 2h;
let Crashes = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("UnexpectedShutdown","OsBugCheck","KernelCrash")
    | project CrashTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, CrashDetails = AdditionalFields;
Crashes
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionAccepted"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize InboundCount = count(), UniqueSrcIPs = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleRemotes = make_set(RemoteIP, 10), TargetPorts = make_set(LocalPort, 10)
              by DeviceId, NetWindowEnd = bin(Timestamp, CrashWindow)
    | where InboundCount > 500 or UniqueSrcIPs > 25
) on DeviceId
| where CrashTime between (NetWindowEnd - CrashWindow .. NetWindowEnd + CrashWindow)
| project CrashTime, DeviceName, InboundCount, UniqueSrcIPs, SampleRemotes, TargetPorts, CrashDetails
| order by CrashTime desc
let CrashWindow = 2h;
let Crashes = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Source in ("Microsoft-Windows-WER-SystemErrorReporting","Save Dump","BugCheck","EventLog")
    | where EventID in (1001, 41, 6008, 1003)
    | project CrashTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription;
Crashes
| join kind=inner (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where CommunicationDirection == "Inbound"
    | summarize InboundCount = count(), UniqueSrcIPs = dcount(SourceIP), SampleRemotes = make_set(SourceIP, 10)
              by DestinationHostName, NetWindowEnd = bin(TimeGenerated, CrashWindow)
    | where InboundCount > 500 or UniqueSrcIPs > 25
) on $left.Computer == $right.DestinationHostName
| where CrashTime between (NetWindowEnd - CrashWindow .. NetWindowEnd + CrashWindow)
| project CrashTime, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription, InboundCount, UniqueSrcIPs, SampleRemotes
| order by CrashTime desc
NETWORK

    | rename All_Traffic.dest as host]

    | rename All_Traffic.dest as host]
| where inbound_count > 1000 OR distinct_src > 50

Python import-hook downloads Bun runtime from oven-sh GitHub release (Hades Campaign) AIInstallation High
Detects Python interpreters fetching the Bun standalone runtime (v1.3.14) from the official oven-sh GitHub release URL — the Hades Campaign hardcodes this exact URL in its obfuscated __init__.py import hook to bootstrap JavaScript payload execution without Node.js. Legitimate Python developer workflows almost never urlretrieve() Bun release zips. Rationale: Anchored on the exact URL string from the deobfuscated import hook: `https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.14/bun-{_m}-{_a}.zip`. Pairing with Python initiating-process eliminates legitimate Bun developer downloads via browser/curl. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/tag/bun-v1.3.14 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer evaluating Bun runtime via Python automation script
  • CI job benchmarking JS runtimes that uses Python to fetch Bun
  • Internal red-team simulating the same TTP
  • Package vendor's own integration tests downloading Bun for cross-runtime validation
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","benchmark","perf_test") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/ci/","/home/runner/work/_temp/"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the Python interpreter; check whether it loaded one of the named packages (ensmallen, embiggen, gpsea, pyphetools, nhmpy, ppkt2synergy, mflux-streamlit) at the corresponding version. Inspect /tmp/b/bun and /tmp/.bun_ran for presence. 2. Contain: Isolate the host. Kill the python and bun processes. Quarantine /tmp/b/, /tmp/b.zip, /tmp/.bun_ran. Rotate any credentials reachable from the host (cloud CLI, SSH, npm/pip tokens). 3. Hunt: Pivot to other hosts that pip-installed the same package versions in the last 30d; check GitHub Actions runners for Runner.Worker memory reads and for outbound DNS to unexpected exfil endpoints.

Bun standalone runtime executes _index.js bootstrapper spawned from Python (Hades) AIInstallation High
Detects the Bun binary executing _index.js with a Python parent — the Hades Campaign drops Bun to /tmp/b/bun and runs `bun run _index.js` to launch its modular AES-GCM-encrypted JavaScript payloads. Legitimate Bun use is parented by shells, IDEs, or package managers — not Python interpreters. Rationale: Article literally specifies the chain: `_s.run([_b, "run", _j], env=dict(_o.environ), check=False)` where `_b = /tmp/b/bun` and `_j = _index.js`. The python→bun parent/child + `_index.js` arg is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a Python-to-Bun integration script
  • Project tooling that ships a vendored Bun binary in /tmp during CI
  • Polyglot benchmark suite running Bun under a Python harness
  • Hades hunter / red team validating prior-campaign IOC
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","tox","unittest") and FolderPath has_any ("/opt/dev/","/home/builder/work/"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Capture parent Python's working directory and __init__.py contents — look for the obfuscated `_O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), '.bun_ran')` exec() string. SHA256 the bun binary against the official oven-sh release hashes. 2. Contain: Isolate. Kill bun + python. Quarantine /tmp/b/bun, /tmp/.bun_ran, /tmp/b.zip, and the _index.js found via the Python search path. 3. Hunt: Search for AsepValueUpdate / cron / launchctl entries pointing at /tmp/b/bun (persistence). Pull Runner.Worker memory-access events and any DNS to non-org domains within 5 min of the bun execution.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName =~ "bun"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "run" and ProcessCommandLine has "_index.js"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/b/","/tmp/","\\Temp\\b\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Hades Campaign once-per-boot marker file /tmp/.bun_ran created by Python AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the `.bun_ran` flag file in the system temp directory by a Python interpreter — the Hades Campaign uses this exact filename as an idempotency marker so the malicious import hook only fires once per boot cycle. The path and filename are hardcoded in the deobfuscated hook. Rationale: `.bun_ran` is a unique, hardcoded filename from the deobfuscated import hook: `_G = _O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), '.bun_ran')` … `open(_G, 'w').close()`. No legitimate software uses this name. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/005/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hades responder writing the marker proactively to inhibit re-execution
  • Forensic analyst replaying the IOC in a sandbox
  • Security tooling that prophylactically drops decoy marker files
  • Researcher reverse-engineering the import hook
Response runbook
1. Triage: Read the parent Python's command line and stack — confirm it imported one of the named packages. Pull __init__.py from the loaded package's installed location. 2. Contain: Isolate. Remove the package via pip uninstall after pulling artifacts. Delete /tmp/b/, /tmp/b.zip, /tmp/.bun_ran. Kill bun/python. 3. Hunt: Sweep for the same file on other hosts via OSQuery / EDR live-response; correlate with pip install events for the affected package versions in the last 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName == ".bun_ran"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","\\Temp\\","/var/folders/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName == ".bun_ran"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","\\Temp\\","/var/folders/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Linux /proc/{pid}/mem read targeting GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (Hades memory scraper) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Python or Bun processes opening /proc/{pid}/maps or /proc/{pid}/mem — the Hades Campaign Linux memory scraper walks runner-process memory mappings and reads plaintext credentials from the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process. Normal user-space tooling rarely touches /proc/*/mem. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'On Linux, the malware walks the memory mappings in /proc/{pid}/maps and directly reads /proc/{pid}/mem to scrape plaintext variables.' The combination of these paths + python/bun is a high-signal credential-access pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/007/ • https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/tree/master/rules/linux
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python performance profiler (py-spy) reading target process memory
  • Custom GC inspector or debugger using ctypes against /proc
  • Memory-forensics tooling running on the host
  • Container runtime introspection script
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","memray","guppy3","objgraph"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the target PID — if it is Runner.Worker, dotnet (GitHub Actions runner), node, or any CI agent process, treat as confirmed. Pull the python script path and confirm origin (PyPI package vs developer-authored). 2. Contain: Isolate the runner. Revoke and rotate all secrets exposed to that runner job (GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC tokens, cloud creds, registry tokens). Disable the affected GitHub Actions workflow. 3. Hunt: Sweep CI/CD fleet for the same /proc/*/mem pattern in last 60d; pull egress flows from any matching runner during the 10 min window after the read; check GitHub audit log for org-secret access from suspect workflows.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath matches regex @"^/proc/[0-9]+/(mem|maps)$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","bun")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/proc/[0-9]+/(mem|maps)$"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","bun")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades Campaign compromised PyPI package install (ensmallen, embiggen, gpsea, et al.) AIDelivery High
Detects installation of any of the seven PyPI packages confirmed compromised in the Hades Campaign at the exact malicious versions. Pip install of these versions is high-confidence initial-access telemetry; downstream import will trigger the obfuscated hook in __init__.py. Rationale: Affected-versions table in the article lists exactly these package@version pairs as the compromised set: mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, ensmallen 0.8.101. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/ • https://pypi.org/project/ensmallen/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genomics/bioinformatics researcher legitimately installing earlier clean versions of these packages
  • CI build for an upstream project that depends transitively on embiggen/ensmallen
  • pip download cache replay
  • Security team intentionally installing the malicious version in an isolated sandbox for analysis
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/malware-analysis/","/home/researcher/sandbox/") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--index-url")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull pip freeze on the host; if any of the seven packages is at the malicious version, confirm. Hash the installed __init__.py and look for the obfuscated `_O.path.join(_T.gettempdir(), '.bun_ran')` exec() string. 2. Contain: Isolate. pip uninstall the affected package; quarantine /tmp/b/, /tmp/.bun_ran. If host is a GitHub Actions runner, revoke any secrets/OIDC tokens reachable from the runner. 3. Hunt: Pivot org-wide on pip install events for these names+versions over 30d; correlate to bun process spawns and /proc/*/mem reads; pull DNS for unusual C2 destinations within 60 min of each install.
let MaliciousPackages = dynamic(["ensmallen==0.8.101","embiggen==0.11.97","gpsea==0.9.14","pyphetools==0.9.120","nhmpy==2.4.7","ppkt2synergy==0.1.1","mflux-streamlit==0.0.3","mflux-streamlit==0.0.4"]);
let PackageNames = dynamic(["ensmallen","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy","mflux-streamlit"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName has_any ("pip","pip3") or (FileName has_any ("python","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has "pip"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again: Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack Targeting AI Coding Agents

StepSecurity
2026-06-09 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 5, 2026, the Miasma worm campaign reached Microsoft's Azure GitHub organizations. GitHub disabled 73 repositories across four Microsoft GitHub organizations after a malicious commit was pushed to the Azure/durabletask repository using a previously compromised contributor account. The attack planted configuration files that execute a credential-harvesting payload when a developer opens the repository in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or VS Code.
